fact_pattern:
Ridgeline Wealth Partners ('Ridgeline'), a registered investment adviser based in Denver, Colorado with approximately $1.4 billion in regulatory assets under management, provides financial planning and portfolio management services through its network of 45 investment adviser representatives. Ridgeline's parent company, Ridgeline Financial Group, also owns Summit Brokerage Services ('Summit'), a registered broker-dealer through which Ridgeline's client trades are executed.

Since 2017, Ridgeline has invested certain advisory clients in mutual fund share classes that pay 12b-1 fees to Summit, even though lower-cost institutional or 'clean' share classes of the same funds were available on the same custodial platform. Ridgeline's Chief Compliance Officer, Denise Hartwell, identified this practice in early 2019 and initiated a review. By Q3 2019, Ridgeline began transitioning approximately 60% of affected accounts to lower-cost share classes, but the remaining 40% — predominantly smaller accounts and accounts holding funds where the institutional share class had a $100,000 minimum that the client could not meet — remained in the higher-cost share classes.

Ridgeline's Form ADV Part 2A, updated in March 2018, contained a general disclosure stating: 'Ridgeline and its affiliates may receive compensation from mutual fund companies, including 12b-1 fees and revenue sharing payments, which create conflicts of interest. Clients should be aware that lower-cost share classes of the same mutual funds may be available.' The disclosure did not specify that Summit, as the affiliated broker-dealer, was the direct recipient of these fees, did not quantify the magnitude of the conflict, and did not explain that Ridgeline had the ability to select share classes that would eliminate the conflict entirely. In its March 2020 ADV update, Ridgeline added more specific language identifying Summit by name and noting the approximate basis-point differential between share classes.

Additionally, Summit received NTF revenue sharing payments from its custodial platform provider, Apex Clearing, based on the volume of client assets invested in certain 'preferred' mutual funds on the NTF platform. Ridgeline's ADV contained no disclosure of this NTF revenue sharing arrangement until the 2020 update. Ridgeline did not participate in the SEC's Share Class Selection Disclosure Initiative, which had a self-reporting deadline of June 12, 2018, because Hartwell believed at the time that the existing ADV disclosure was adequate and that the firm's partial remediation efforts demonstrated good faith. In total, the estimated excess fees borne by clients from the higher-cost share classes between 2017 and the completion of the transition in mid-2021 were approximately $1.8 million.
analysis:
The SEC's enforcement theory would focus on Ridgeline's fiduciary duty under Sections 206(1) and 206(2) of the Investment Advisers Act, arguing that the firm's pre-2020 disclosure was materially inadequate. Under the standard articulated in SEC v. Capital Gains Research Bureau (1963), an investment adviser has an affirmative obligation to make full and fair disclosure of all material conflicts of interest, and the SEC has consistently held that generic references to 'compensation from mutual fund companies' are insufficient when the adviser has the ability and obligation to select the lowest-cost share class for clients. The SEC would argue that Ridgeline's failure to identify Summit by name, quantify the conflict, or explain that lower-cost alternatives were readily available rendered the disclosure misleading. The failure to disclose NTF revenue sharing at all until 2020 would further support the enforcement theory. The SEC would also likely argue that Ridgeline's failure to self-report under the SCSD Initiative, combined with the two-year delay in completing remediation, demonstrates a lack of the good faith that might otherwise mitigate sanctions.

Ridgeline's defense would emphasize several factors: (1) the firm did include a general conflict disclosure beginning in 2018 that specifically referenced 12b-1 fees and the availability of lower-cost share classes, which arguably put clients on notice of the conflict; (2) the firm self-identified the issue through its compliance program and began proactive remediation before any SEC examination or inquiry; (3) the 40% of accounts that remained in higher-cost share classes had legitimate operational reasons (minimum investment thresholds) rather than revenue motivation; and (4) the firm voluntarily enhanced its disclosures in 2020. Defense counsel would argue that the disclosure, while imperfect, was not fraudulent or deliberately misleading, and that the firm's conduct represents at most a technical compliance deficiency rather than a fiduciary breach — particularly given that the industry standard for such disclosures was evolving rapidly during 2017-2019 and many firms had similarly general language. The defense would further note that the SCSD Initiative was voluntary and that declining to self-report cannot itself constitute a violation.
why_borderline: This scenario sits in a genuine gray zone because Ridgeline did provide some disclosure of the 12b-1 fee conflict — unlike firms that provided no disclosure whatsoever — but the disclosure lacked the specificity the SEC has increasingly demanded. The firm also engaged in partial self-correction before any regulatory action, which complicates the enforcement narrative. The core ambiguity is whether a general disclosure that references 12b-1 fees and acknowledges the availability of lower-cost share classes satisfies an adviser's fiduciary duty, or whether the duty requires granular, quantified disclosure identifying the specific affiliated entity and the precise economic incentive. Post-SCSD Initiative enforcement actions have largely targeted firms with no disclosure or egregiously deficient disclosure, and Ridgeline's pre-2020 language falls in the uncertain middle ground. Additionally, the legitimate operational justification for the remaining 40% of unremediated accounts (share class minimums) introduces factual complexity that cuts against a finding of willful misconduct.
borderline_factors: Ridgeline provided general but arguably insufficient 12b-1 fee disclosure before 2020, creating ambiguity about whether the disclosure met the full and fair standard under Section 206(2)

The firm proactively identified the issue and began remediation before any SEC examination, but took approximately two years to complete the transition and never self-reported under the SCSD Initiative

Approximately 40% of unremediated accounts had a facially legitimate operational reason (institutional share class minimums) for remaining in higher-cost share classes, complicating the inference of conflicted motivation

NTF revenue sharing was entirely undisclosed until 2020, but the materiality of NTF payments relative to 12b-1 fees and the evolving industry awareness of NTF conflicts create ambiguity about whether the omission was negligent or reckless
likely_outcome: A regulator would most likely find a violation of Sections 206(2) and 206(4) of the Advisers Act, along with Rule 206(4)-7 (compliance policies and procedures), but would credit the firm's partial remediation and self-identification of the issue as significant mitigating factors. The SEC would likely pursue a settled administrative proceeding rather than litigation, imposing a censure, a cease-and-desist order, and a civil penalty in the range of $250,000-$500,000 — meaningfully less than the $1.8 million in estimated client harm, reflecting credit for the firm's remedial efforts. The SEC would also require disgorgement of the $1.8 million plus prejudgment interest, returned to affected clients. The outcome would be notably less severe than cases involving no disclosure and no remediation, but the SEC would reject the argument that the general disclosure was sufficient, consistent with its post-SCSD Initiative enforcement posture that generic conflict language does not satisfy an adviser's fiduciary obligations. The NTF non-disclosure would be treated as a separate but related violation strengthening the SEC's overall case.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act of 1940 §§206(1), 206(2), 206(4); Rule 206(4)-7 (compliance policies and procedures); SEC Share Class Selection Disclosure Initiative (2018); SEC v. Capital Gains Research Bureau, 375 U.S. 180 (1963) (full and fair disclosure standard); Investment Company Act Rule 12b-1; Form ADV Part 2A disclosure requirements (Item 12 - Brokerage Practices; Item 14 - Client Referrals and Other Compensation)

fact_pattern:
Marcus Devereaux, a 45-year-old former Series 7 licensed broker whose registration lapsed in 2020, organizes a group called the 'Meridian Wealth Collective' in early 2023 with twelve close friends and family members in Newark, New Jersey. The group pools funds into a single Schwab brokerage account held in the name of Meridian Wealth Collective LLC, a New Jersey LLC formed by Devereaux. Each member contributes between $5,000 and $25,000, totaling approximately $185,000. Devereaux makes all trading decisions for the group, primarily investing in blue-chip equities, covered call options, and investment-grade corporate bonds. The group's operating agreement states that Devereaux will receive no direct management fee, but will receive a 'coordinator stipend' of $200 per month to cover his time and administrative costs, plus reimbursement of actual expenses. The agreement also states that if the portfolio returns exceed 8% annually, Devereaux will receive 10% of the excess gains as a 'performance allocation.' Over the course of 2023, the portfolio returns approximately 14%, and Devereaux receives $2,400 in monthly stipends plus approximately $1,110 in performance allocation.

Devereaux does not register as an investment adviser with the SEC or with New Jersey's Bureau of Securities. He does not provide written disclosures about his background, conflicts of interest, or risk factors. However, he holds quarterly in-person meetings with all members where he reviews the portfolio, explains his strategy, and answers questions. He also sends monthly email summaries. He does not solicit new members and in fact turns away three acquaintances who ask to join, telling them the group is 'closed to friends and family only.' None of the twelve members have complained, and the group's returns have been reasonable and consistent with market performance. In mid-2024, one of the original members goes through a divorce, and her estranged spouse's attorney, during discovery, identifies the Meridian Wealth Collective arrangement and reports it to the SEC as a potential unregistered investment adviser and unregistered securities offering.
analysis:
The SEC would likely analyze whether Devereaux meets the definition of 'investment adviser' under Section 202(a)(11) of the Investment Advisers Act — a person who, for compensation, engages in the business of advising others about the value of securities. The three-prong Lowe v. SEC test requires: (1) providing advice about securities, (2) being in the business of doing so, and (3) receiving compensation for the advice. Devereaux clearly satisfies the first prong — he makes all investment decisions for the group's pooled assets. The compensation prong is where genuine tension arises: the $200 monthly stipend is nominally for 'coordination,' and the performance allocation could be characterized either as adviser compensation or as a legitimate profit-sharing arrangement among co-investors. The SEC has historically taken a broad view of compensation, finding that any economic benefit — even indirect — can satisfy this element. The 'business' prong also presents ambiguity: Devereaux manages money for only one small, closed group of personal relationships and has affirmatively refused to expand, which arguably places him closer to an informal family arrangement than a 'business.'

On the other side, a defense attorney would invoke the SEC's own guidance on investment clubs, particularly the no-action letter tradition (e.g., the 1995 Investment Club guidance) suggesting that genuine investment clubs where all members participate in decisions and share control are not investment companies or advisory relationships requiring registration. However, Devereaux's arrangement departs from the typical investment club model because the members do not participate in individual investment decisions — Devereaux exercises sole discretion. The defense would counter that the operating agreement was freely negotiated among sophisticated adults, that the amounts are modest, that no public solicitation occurred, and that the performance allocation aligns Devereaux's incentives with the group's interests rather than creating the kind of conflict that registration requirements are designed to address. The defense might also argue that Section 203(b)(3) provides a private adviser exemption (though this was narrowed by Dodd-Frank), or that the arrangement functions as a single pooled vehicle, not an advisory relationship with multiple 'clients.'
why_borderline: This scenario sits in a genuine gray zone because it combines features of both a legitimate informal investment club (small size, personal relationships, closed membership, modest amounts, no public solicitation) with features that typically trigger investment adviser status (sole discretionary control by one person, compensation tied to performance, pooled assets in a single entity, no shared decision-making). The SEC's historical guidance on investment clubs contemplates shared decision-making among all members, but is less clear about arrangements where a single competent member is delegated authority by unanimous consent. The compensation structure — a nominal monthly stipend plus modest performance allocation — occupies an uncertain middle ground between true compensation for advisory services and a reasonable arrangement for reimbursing a volunteer coordinator. Additionally, Devereaux's lapsed broker registration creates ambiguity about whether he should have known registration was required, or whether his professional background actually made the arrangement more competent and less risky for participants.
borderline_factors: Sole discretionary trading authority vested in one member versus unanimous delegation by informed co-investors in a closed group
Compensation structure that blends nominal administrative stipend with performance-based allocation — is this advisory compensation or profit-sharing among co-investors?
Closed group of 12 friends and family with no solicitation versus SEC's broad interpretation of 'business' standard under the three-prong investment adviser test
Absence of formal written disclosures about risks and conflicts versus quarterly in-person meetings with full transparency and no complaints from any participant
likely_outcome: The SEC would likely conclude that Devereaux was acting as an unregistered investment adviser, primarily because of his sole discretionary control over investment decisions and the compensation he received, which together satisfy all three prongs of the investment adviser definition. However, the enforcement response would likely be measured — the SEC would probably issue a deficiency letter or seek a consent order requiring Devereaux to cease advisory activity or register, rather than pursuing a fraud-based enforcement action. The absence of investor harm, the modest scale, the closed nature of the group, and the reasonable investment returns all cut against aggressive enforcement. A court reviewing the matter would likely find technical violations of registration requirements but would be unlikely to impose severe sanctions. The key distinguishing factor from the Pierre case in the source document is the absence of unrealistic return promises, misrepresentations, misappropriation, or Ponzi-like features — this is a competence and registration case, not a fraud case.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act §§ 202(a)(11) (definition of investment adviser), 203(a) (registration requirement), 206(1)-(2) (antifraud provisions — duty of disclosure); SEC v. Lowe, 472 U.S. 181 (1985) (three-prong test for investment adviser status); Goldstein v. SEC, 451 F.3d 873 (D.C. Cir. 2006) (defining 'client' in pooled vehicle context); Investment Company Act § 3(c)(1) (private fund exemption for fewer than 100 investors); New Jersey Uniform Securities Law § 49:3-56 (state investment adviser registration); SEC Staff No-Action Letters on investment clubs (1995 guidance)

fact_pattern:
Northbridge Capital Advisors, LLC ('Northbridge') is a registered investment adviser managing approximately $18 billion for institutional clients, pension funds, and high-net-worth individuals. In March 2023, Northbridge's Chief Investment Officer, Marcus Hale, receives a $15 million unsecured personal loan from Sanderson Family Office ('Sanderson'), one of Northbridge's largest advisory clients with approximately $900 million under management. The loan carries a below-market interest rate of 2.1% (compared to prevailing rates of approximately 6.5%) and is extended so that Hale can personally co-invest alongside Northbridge's parent company, Northbridge Holdings Group, in a private credit fund acquisition. Hale discloses the loan to Northbridge's General Counsel, Rebecca Tsao, who reviews the arrangement and determines that because the loan is a personal financial transaction between Hale and Sanderson — not a transaction involving Northbridge's advisory accounts — it does not need to be disclosed to Northbridge's other advisory clients. Tsao does, however, require Hale to file an updated personal securities transaction report under Northbridge's Code of Ethics, which Hale does.

Over the following nine months, Northbridge allocates investment opportunities in two structured credit transactions to multiple client accounts, including Sanderson's account. In both transactions, Sanderson receives allocation on terms that are materially identical to those offered to other Northbridge clients of comparable size and risk profile — there is no evidence that Sanderson received preferential allocation, better pricing, or priority in any respect. However, Northbridge's other clients are never informed that Hale has an outstanding $15 million personal loan from Sanderson. None of Northbridge's Form ADV disclosures or client communications reference the loan or the potential conflict it creates.

In early 2024, during a routine SEC examination, staff examiners discover the loan through a review of Hale's personal financial disclosure filings. The examiners note that Northbridge's compliance policies and procedures manual contains a provision requiring disclosure to clients of 'material conflicts of interest arising from personal financial relationships between Northbridge personnel and advisory clients,' but the manual does not specifically define what constitutes a 'material' personal financial relationship or prescribe a specific disclosure mechanism. Tsao explains to examiners that she conducted a conflicts analysis and concluded that because no client was disadvantaged — allocations were fair and no favoritism was shown — the conflict was theoretical rather than actual, and therefore not 'material' within the meaning of the firm's policies or the Advisers Act. Northbridge's compliance committee meeting minutes from April 2023 reflect a brief discussion of the loan, with the notation: 'GC reviewed and determined no client disclosure required at this time; will monitor for actual conflicts.'
analysis:
The SEC's position, grounded in Sections 206(1) and 206(2) of the Investment Advisers Act, would likely be that Northbridge had an affirmative fiduciary obligation to disclose the Hale-Sanderson loan to all advisory clients, regardless of whether any client was actually harmed. The Commission has consistently held that an investment adviser's fiduciary duty encompasses full and fair disclosure of all material conflicts of interest, and that the existence of a substantial personal financial relationship between a senior investment professional and one advisory client creates an inherent conflict — the adviser may consciously or unconsciously favor that client's interests to preserve the personal financial benefit. Under SEC v. Capital Gains Research Bureau (1963), the Supreme Court established that the Advisers Act reflects a congressional intent to eliminate conflicts of interest, and that an adviser need not actually engage in fraudulent conduct for an undisclosed conflict to constitute a violation. The Guggenheim Partners enforcement action is directly analogous: the SEC found a breach of fiduciary duty based on the mere failure to disclose a senior executive's $50 million loan from a client, without requiring proof that other clients were actually disadvantaged.

Northbridge's defense, however, has genuine force. Unlike the Guggenheim matter, Northbridge can demonstrate through contemporaneous documentation that its General Counsel conducted a real-time conflicts analysis, that the loan was internally reported under the Code of Ethics, that the compliance committee discussed and documented the issue, and — most critically — that no client received preferential treatment in any allocation or transaction. Defense counsel would argue that the Advisers Act does not impose strict liability for every undisclosed personal relationship, but rather requires materiality — and that a conflict which is identified, monitored, and produces no actual favoritism is not material to clients' investment decisions. The firm would further argue that the SEC's position, taken to its logical extreme, would require disclosure of virtually any personal financial interaction between adviser personnel and clients, creating an unworkable compliance burden. Northbridge could also point to the fact that its compliance manual's ambiguity regarding the definition of 'material' personal financial relationships reflects genuine interpretive difficulty, not willful evasion.
why_borderline: This scenario sits in a genuine gray zone because the SEC's post-Capital Gains Research Bureau jurisprudence strongly favors prophylactic disclosure of conflicts, yet the specific question of whether an undisclosed personal loan that produces no demonstrable favoritism constitutes a 'material' conflict requiring client disclosure remains doctrinally unsettled. The Guggenheim order itself was a settlement, not a litigated decision, meaning its precedential value is limited. Northbridge's contemporaneous compliance review, internal documentation, and demonstrably fair allocation practices distinguish it from cases involving complete compliance failures. The core tension is between the SEC's expansive reading of fiduciary duty as requiring disclosure of potential conflicts irrespective of harm, versus the defense position that materiality is a necessary element and should be assessed based on whether the conflict actually affected or could reasonably be expected to affect client outcomes.
borderline_factors: The loan was internally disclosed and documented under the Code of Ethics, but not disclosed to other advisory clients — raising the question of whether internal compliance review can substitute for client-facing disclosure

No evidence of actual preferential treatment or harm to any client, which undermines the materiality of the undisclosed conflict but does not negate the fiduciary duty to disclose potential conflicts under SEC precedent

The firm's compliance manual required disclosure of 'material' conflicts from personal financial relationships but did not define materiality thresholds, creating ambiguity about whether the firm's own policies were violated

The below-market interest rate on the loan (2.1% vs. 6.5% prevailing) suggests the relationship conferred a substantial personal benefit on the CIO, strengthening the argument that the conflict was material even if no client was harmed
likely_outcome: The SEC would likely pursue an enforcement action and prevail, either through settlement or adjudication. The Commission's consistent position — reinforced by the Guggenheim precedent and multiple analogous cases — is that the failure to disclose a senior executive's substantial personal financial relationship with an advisory client constitutes a per se breach of fiduciary duty under Sections 206(1) and 206(2), regardless of whether other clients suffered actual harm. The below-market loan terms would be cited as evidence that the conflict was economically significant. However, the sanctions would likely be mitigated by Northbridge's internal compliance efforts — the contemporaneous legal review, Code of Ethics filing, and compliance committee documentation suggest negligence rather than intentional concealment. The likely resolution would be a settled administrative proceeding with a censure, a civil penalty in the range of $1-5 million (significantly less than Guggenheim's penalty given the smaller loan amount and documented compliance efforts), and an undertaking to revise compliance policies and procedures to establish bright-line disclosure obligations for personal financial relationships between personnel and clients.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act of 1940 §§206(1), 206(2) (anti-fraud and fiduciary duty provisions); §206(4) and Rule 206(4)-7 (compliance policies and procedures); §204 and Rule 204-2 (books and records requirements); SEC v. Capital Gains Research Bureau, Inc., 375 U.S. 180 (1963) (fiduciary duty to disclose conflicts); In re Guggenheim Partners Investment Management, LLC, IA Release No. 4163 (Aug. 10, 2015) (undisclosed executive loan from advisory client)

fact_pattern:
Meridian Capital Advisors Ltd. ('Meridian') is a London-based investment advisory firm founded in 2018 by Claire Ashworth, a veteran portfolio manager who previously spent 15 years at a major U.S. asset management firm. Meridian is registered with the UK Financial Conduct Authority and manages approximately $4.2 billion in assets, primarily for European institutional clients including pension funds, sovereign wealth entities, and family offices.

Meridian is not registered as an investment adviser with the SEC. However, Meridian maintains a 'participating affiliate' arrangement with its New York-based affiliate, Meridian US Partners LLC ('Meridian US'), which is SEC-registered. Under this arrangement, certain London-based portfolio managers at Meridian provide sub-advisory research and model portfolio recommendations that Meridian US personnel review and may implement for Meridian US's American clients. Meridian US has approximately $800 million in assets under management from U.S. institutional investors.

In March 2024, Claire Ashworth traveled to New York to attend an industry conference. During the trip, she had three dinners with existing European clients who happened to be in New York simultaneously. At two of those dinners, representatives of U.S.-based pension funds — the Ohio Municipal Workers Retirement System and the Texas Teachers' Endowment Fund — were also present as guests of the European clients. During wide-ranging conversations about global macro conditions and emerging market opportunities, Ashworth shared specific investment views, including her conviction that certain Brazilian and Indian equities were significantly undervalued, naming specific securities and price targets. She did not formally solicit business from the U.S. pension representatives, but she did provide her business card, and one U.S. pension representative later emailed her directly requesting a detailed investment memorandum on emerging market opportunities. Ashworth responded from London with a 14-page research document, after which the Ohio Municipal Workers Retirement System invested $45 million through Meridian US.

Meridian's compliance officer, David Renwick, had approved Ashworth's conference attendance but was not informed of the dinner meetings with U.S. institutional investors. The participating affiliate arrangement's compliance manual specifies that London-based personnel may not 'solicit or provide personalized investment advice to U.S. persons' without Meridian US supervision, but it does not clearly define whether sharing market views in a social setting constitutes 'personalized investment advice.' Meridian has no written policies addressing incidental contacts with U.S. persons during international travel.
analysis:
The SEC could argue that Ashworth's conduct constituted unregistered investment advisory activity directed at U.S. persons in violation of Sections 206 and 207 of the Investment Advisers Act. Under the functional definition of 'investment adviser' in Section 202(a)(11), the key question is whether Ashworth was 'engaged in the business' of advising U.S. persons about securities for compensation. The SEC has historically taken a broad view of what constitutes advisory activity, and Ashworth's provision of specific security recommendations with price targets — followed by a detailed written memorandum sent directly to a U.S. pension fund — could be characterized as a classic advisory relationship. The fact that the $45 million investment flowed through the registered Meridian US entity does not necessarily sanitize the unregistered solicitation that preceded it. The SEC staff's position, even post-Unibanco, has been that activities directed at U.S. clients or having effects on U.S. investors remain subject to Advisers Act regulation. Moreover, the participating affiliate framework requires that London-based personnel operate under the supervision of the SEC-registered entity, and Ashworth's unsupervised communications arguably violated both the spirit and letter of that arrangement.

Meridian's defense would emphasize several points. First, the dinner conversations were social and incidental — Ashworth did not seek out U.S. investors, they were guests of her existing European clients. Second, sharing general macro views and investment themes, even with specific security names, at a social dinner does not constitute 'personalized investment advice' absent a formal advisory relationship. Third, when the U.S. pension fund affirmatively reached out, Ashworth responded from London — implicating the Unibanco line of no-action relief suggesting that a foreign adviser's activities conducted outside the United States with respect to non-clients are not subject to the full Advisers Act regulatory scheme. Fourth, the actual investment was properly channeled through the SEC-registered Meridian US, which conducted its own independent diligence and maintained the advisory relationship. The defense would argue this is precisely the kind of organic, cross-border interaction that the SEC's evolving position — moving toward regulating U.S. activities and protecting U.S. investors from harm rather than asserting global jurisdiction — was designed to accommodate.
why_borderline: This scenario sits at the precise intersection of several unsettled questions in cross-border advisory regulation. The Unibanco no-action framework contemplates relief for foreign advisers serving non-U.S. clients from outside the United States, but Ashworth's conduct involved direct, in-person contact with U.S. institutional investors on U.S. soil, followed by substantive written communications that arguably initiated an advisory relationship outside the participating affiliate framework. Yet the contacts were genuinely incidental rather than planned solicitations, and the investment was ultimately processed through proper registered channels. The SEC's evolving position on extraterritorial application of the Advisers Act — moving from asserting worldwide jurisdiction to a more effects-based, U.S.-activity-focused approach — creates genuine ambiguity about whether this pattern of conduct crosses the line. Reasonable compliance officers and securities lawyers could disagree sharply on whether social conversation shading into specific investment recommendations, followed by responsive (not initiated) written research, constitutes the kind of U.S.-directed advisory activity the SEC intends to regulate.
borderline_factors: Whether sharing specific security recommendations with price targets in a social setting constitutes 'personalized investment advice' or general market commentary not triggering Advisers Act obligations
Whether Ashworth's physical presence in the United States during the initial conversations transforms otherwise permissible foreign adviser conduct into regulable U.S. advisory activity

Whether the responsive nature of the follow-up research memorandum (sent from London in response to an unsolicited request from the U.S. pension fund) falls within the Unibanco no-action framework for foreign adviser activities outside the United States

Whether channeling the resulting investment through the SEC-registered participating affiliate (Meridian US) retroactively cures any compliance deficiency in the originating contact, or whether the unregistered solicitation taints the entire transaction
likely_outcome: The SEC would likely pursue this as an administrative proceeding rather than a fraud action, focusing on supervisory failures and technical violations of the participating affiliate framework rather than substantive fraud under Sections 206(1) and 206(2). The most probable resolution would be a settled administrative order requiring Meridian to enhance its compliance procedures for cross-border contacts, pay a modest civil penalty ($150,000-$300,000 range), and retain an independent compliance consultant. The SEC would likely emphasize the gap between Meridian's written policies and actual practice, and the failure of compliance officer Renwick to establish adequate controls over incidental U.S. contacts. However, the SEC would face significant litigation risk if Meridian contested the action, because the incidental and social nature of the initial contacts, the responsive character of the written memorandum, and the proper channeling of the investment through registered entities all provide substantial defenses. A contested proceeding could go either way before an ALJ, and the outcome would likely turn on whether the adjudicator viewed Ashworth's dinner conversations as substantive advisory activity or casual social discourse — a genuinely fact-intensive determination.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act of 1940 §§202(a)(11) (definition of investment adviser), 203(a) (registration requirement), 206(1)-(2) (anti-fraud provisions), 207 (material misstatements in registration); SEC no-action letters including Uniao de Bancos de Brasileiros S.A. (1992), Mercury Asset Management plc (1993), Kleinwort Benson Investment Management Ltd. (1994) (participating affiliate framework); SEC Release IA-1092 (definition of 'engaged in the business'); 1992 SEC Staff Report 'Protecting Investors: A Half Century of Investment Company Regulation'

fact_pattern:
Meridian Wealth Partners, LLC ('Meridian') is a SEC-registered investment adviser based in Hartford, Connecticut, with approximately $380 million in assets under management. Meridian is co-managed by its two principals, Catherine Hollis and Brian Vasquez, who share discretionary investment authority over client accounts.

In 2019, Hollis served as a paid advisory board member for NovaBridge Technologies, Inc. ('NovaBridge'), a publicly traded micro-cap company. Her engagement lasted 14 months, during which she received $24,000 in cash compensation and was granted 30,000 restricted shares of NovaBridge common stock subject to a one-year lockup. Hollis's advisory board term formally ended in March 2020, and the restricted shares fully vested and became unrestricted in March 2021.

Beginning in September 2021 — six months after the shares became unrestricted — Vasquez, exercising his independent discretionary authority, began purchasing NovaBridge shares for approximately 40 Meridian client accounts. The purchases were modest (typically 500-2,000 shares per account, representing less than 2% of each portfolio). Vasquez maintains he identified NovaBridge through his own independent screening process, which flagged the company based on revenue growth metrics and a favorable analyst report from a regional broker-dealer. Vasquez states he was unaware of Hollis's prior advisory board service until after an internal compliance review flagged the purchases in January 2022.

Hollis still held her 30,000 shares of NovaBridge during the period Vasquez was purchasing for clients. Meridian's Form ADV Part 2A disclosed generally that 'principals and employees may hold personal positions in securities also held in client accounts,' but did not specifically disclose Hollis's prior consulting relationship with NovaBridge, her share ownership, or the circumstances under which she acquired the shares. Meridian's compliance manual required employees to report outside business activities, and Hollis had reported her NovaBridge advisory board service in 2019, but no follow-up compliance review was conducted when the relationship ended or when the shares vested. When the compliance officer flagged the NovaBridge purchases in January 2022, Meridian promptly added specific disclosure about Hollis's prior relationship and current holdings to its brochure supplement and notified affected clients.
analysis:
The SEC's enforcement action in Strategic Planning Group establishes that investment advisers violate Section 206(2) of the Advisers Act when they fail to disclose material conflicts of interest arising from principals' financial connections to issuers whose securities are purchased for client accounts. The central question here is whether Hollis's expired advisory board relationship and residual stock ownership created a conflict sufficiently material to require specific disclosure, particularly when the investment decisions were made independently by a different principal. The SEC could argue that Hollis's 30,000-share position created an inherent incentive for Meridian — as an entity — to support NovaBridge's stock price through client purchases, and that the failure to specifically disclose the prior relationship and current holdings was a breach of fiduciary duty regardless of whether Vasquez acted independently. The SEC has consistently taken the position that advisers must err on the side of full disclosure and that generic ADV language about personal holdings is insufficient when a principal has a specific, compensatory history with an issuer.

Defense counsel would argue several distinguishing factors. Unlike in SPG, where the same principals who held the conflicted relationship were the ones directing client investments, here the purchasing principal (Vasquez) was independent and allegedly unaware of Hollis's connection. The advisory board relationship had terminated 18 months before the first client purchase, making it a historical rather than ongoing conflict. Hollis's 30,000 shares in a publicly traded company represent a relatively modest economic interest, and the generic ADV disclosure about personal holdings, while not specific, was not misleading. Defense counsel would also emphasize the firm's prompt remediation once the issue was identified. The defense would frame this as, at worst, a compliance process failure rather than a substantive fraud or breach of fiduciary duty.
why_borderline: This case sits in a genuine gray zone because it tests the boundaries of how far back in time a conflict-generating relationship remains material, whether a conflict held by one principal must be imputed to independent investment decisions by another principal, and whether generic disclosure in Form ADV adequately addresses what the SEC might view as requiring specific disclosure. The SPG precedent involved ongoing relationships and the same individuals making both the conflicted and investment decisions — here, both of those factors are attenuated. Reasonable compliance professionals would disagree about whether a terminated advisory board relationship creates an ongoing disclosure obligation, and whether Vasquez's independent decision-making breaks the causal chain the SEC typically relies on in these cases.
borderline_factors: The conflict-generating advisory board relationship had terminated 18 months before client purchases began, creating ambiguity about temporal materiality
The investment decisions were made by a different principal (Vasquez) who claims independent analysis and no knowledge of Hollis's prior relationship
Hollis retained 30,000 unrestricted shares — an ongoing economic interest that could be seen as creating a latent incentive even after the formal relationship ended
Generic ADV disclosure about personal holdings existed but did not specifically identify the prior compensatory relationship with the issuer or the circumstances of share acquisition
likely_outcome: The SEC would likely pursue this as a settled administrative proceeding resulting in a censure of Meridian, modest civil penalties, and a cease-and-desist order under Section 206(2), but probably would not seek bars against either individual. The SEC's position would be that an adviser has an affirmative obligation to disclose any principal's compensatory relationship with an issuer whose securities are purchased for clients, regardless of temporal distance or which principal made the investment decision, and that generic ADV language is insufficient. However, the mitigating factors — terminated relationship, independent decision-maker, prompt remediation, small position sizes — would significantly reduce sanctions compared to the SPG matter. A court reviewing this de novo might be more sympathetic to the defense, particularly on the question of whether Vasquez's independent decision-making negates the scienter or negligence element, but the SEC's broad reading of fiduciary duty under Section 206(2) (which requires only negligence) would likely prevail on the disclosure obligation itself.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act §206(2) (fraud by investment adviser through negligent conduct); Investment Advisers Act §207 (material misstatements or omissions in filings); SEC Form ADV Part 2A disclosure requirements (Item 11 — conflicts of interest; Item 6 — outside business activities); Investment Advisers Act §206(4) and Rule 206(4)-7 (compliance policies and procedures); SEC guidance on fiduciary duty and full disclosure obligations of investment advisers

fact_pattern:
Meridian Capital Advisors LLC ('Meridian') is a registered investment adviser based in Denver, Colorado, managing approximately $340 million in regulatory assets under management, primarily for high-net-worth individuals and small institutional clients. In January 2023, after the November 4, 2022 compliance deadline for the Amended Marketing Rule, Meridian redesigned its website to feature a sophisticated interactive tool called the 'Portfolio Scenario Builder,' which allows users to input various asset allocation weightings and generates hypothetical backtested performance results showing how those allocations would have performed over 1-, 3-, 5-, and 10-year trailing periods using actual index and model portfolio return data.

To comply with Rule 206(4)-1(d), Meridian implemented an access-gating mechanism: before accessing the Portfolio Scenario Builder, website visitors must complete a brief online questionnaire that asks (1) whether the visitor is an existing Meridian client, prospective client, or financial professional; (2) the visitor's approximate investable assets (under $250K, $250K-$1M, $1M-$5M, or $5M+); and (3) the visitor's general investment objective (capital preservation, balanced growth, aggressive growth, or income). Based on the responses, the tool auto-selects which model portfolios and scenario ranges are displayed, theoretically tailoring the hypothetical performance to the respondent's stated financial profile. However, the questionnaire does not verify any of the inputs, there is no identity verification, and a visitor who selects 'under $250K' and 'capital preservation' is still shown hypothetical returns for conservative model portfolios that include alternative investments with $500,000 minimums that Meridian only offers to clients with $2 million or more in investable assets.

Meridian's Chief Compliance Officer, Rachel Fontaine, reviewed the system before launch and approved it, documenting in a compliance memorandum that the gating questionnaire constituted 'reasonable policies and procedures designed to ensure relevance to the likely financial situation and investment objectives of the intended audience.' The memorandum referenced the SEC's Adopting Release and noted that the tool's design represented a 'good faith, technology-forward approach' to the new requirement. However, Fontaine did not address the fact that the questionnaire responses were unverified, that the conservative portfolio options shown to lower-asset respondents contained investment minimums far exceeding the respondent's stated assets, or that the tool was accessible to anyone on the open internet without any requirement that the visitor have a pre-existing relationship with Meridian.

During a routine SEC examination in mid-2023, staff raised concerns about the adequacy of Meridian's policies and procedures, noting that the self-reported questionnaire with no verification mechanism may not satisfy the rule's requirement that hypothetical performance be 'relevant to the likely financial situation and investment objectives of the intended audience.' Meridian's outside counsel, David Ashworth of Klein & Ashworth LLP, responded that the Amended Marketing Rule does not require identity verification or mandate any particular gating methodology, and that the SEC's own Adopting Release contemplated a principles-based approach to relevance that accommodates technology-driven solutions like Meridian's.
analysis:
The SEC's strongest argument is that Meridian's policies and procedures are not 'reasonably designed' to ensure hypothetical performance relevance because the self-reported questionnaire is trivially easy to circumvent, contains no verification, and — critically — still displays hypothetical performance for investment products that are objectively irrelevant to a respondent's stated financial situation (e.g., showing alternative investment returns with $500K minimums to someone who reports under $250K in investable assets). The Hansen & Associates enforcement action demonstrates the Commission's willingness to bring cases against advisers who display hypothetical performance on public websites without adequate relevance-filtering mechanisms. Staff could argue that the internal logic failure — showing inaccessible products to self-identified lower-asset visitors — is evidence that the policies were not reasonably designed regardless of the gating mechanism's existence. The Commission could also point to the Adopting Release's emphasis that hypothetical performance shown on an unrestricted public website requires particularly robust controls given the breadth of the potential audience.

Meridian's defense is substantial, however. The Amended Marketing Rule is explicitly principles-based and does not prescribe specific gating mechanisms, verification requirements, or particular technologies. The Adopting Release acknowledged that advisers would need flexibility in determining how to ensure relevance and did not mandate identity verification or restrict the use of self-reported questionnaires. Meridian implemented a documented compliance framework, the CCO conducted a review, and the tool does filter content based on stated investor characteristics — a meaningful step beyond what Hansen & Associates did (which was essentially nothing). Counsel Ashworth would argue that 'reasonably designed' does not mean 'perfectly effective' and that the mismatch between stated assets and product minimums is a refinement issue, not a fundamental compliance failure. He would further argue that the SEC risks imposing a prescriptive standard through enforcement that it deliberately declined to adopt through rulemaking.
why_borderline: This scenario sits in the gray zone because the Amended Marketing Rule deliberately adopted a principles-based standard ('reasonably designed') rather than prescribing specific compliance mechanisms for hypothetical performance relevance. Meridian implemented a documented process with technology-based filtering — putting it meaningfully ahead of the Hansen & Associates baseline of no policies at all — but the process has identifiable logical gaps (showing irrelevant products, no verification) that undermine its effectiveness. Reasonable compliance professionals could disagree on whether a self-reported, unverified online questionnaire with content-filtering logic constitutes 'reasonable' policies and procedures, particularly when the tool is accessible on the open internet. The question ultimately turns on how much rigor the SEC expects under a standard it intentionally left flexible, and whether the existence of a facially plausible but imperfect system satisfies the rule or whether specific demonstrable failures in the filtering logic transform an adequate system into an inadequate one.
borderline_factors: The Amended Marketing Rule is principles-based and does not prescribe specific gating mechanisms, verification requirements, or technology solutions for ensuring hypothetical performance relevance

Meridian implemented documented policies, CCO review, and a technology-based filtering system — distinguishing it from Hansen & Associates' complete absence of procedures — but the system contains identifiable logical gaps

The self-reported questionnaire lacks any verification mechanism, meaning anyone can access any hypothetical performance data by simply selecting different responses, undermining the relevance-filtering purpose

The tool displays hypothetical returns for products with investment minimums far exceeding a respondent's self-reported investable assets, creating an objective mismatch between displayed performance and the stated financial situation of the viewer
likely_outcome: The SEC examination staff would likely issue a deficiency letter requiring Meridian to remediate the specific logical gaps in its filtering system rather than pursuing a formal enforcement action. The existence of documented policies, CCO review, and a functional (if imperfect) gating mechanism likely puts Meridian above the enforcement threshold established by Hansen & Associates, which involved essentially no compliance effort. However, if Meridian failed to remediate after receiving the deficiency letter, or if the SEC determined to use this case to establish a higher floor for what constitutes 'reasonably designed' policies for public website hypothetical performance, a formal action under Section 206(4) and Rule 206(4)-1(d) would be plausible. The most likely resolution is a negotiated remediation: Meridian agrees to implement verification enhancements, remove or restrict products from display where minimums exceed stated assets, and potentially add a pre-qualification step for non-client visitors — without an enforcement proceeding or sanctions.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act §206(4); Advisers Act Rule 206(4)-1(d) (Amended Marketing Rule — hypothetical performance requirements); Advisers Act Rule 206(4)-1(d)(6) (requirement that hypothetical performance be relevant to the likely financial situation and investment objectives of the intended audience and that the adviser adopt and implement policies and procedures reasonably designed to ensure such relevance); Investment Adviser Marketing, Release No. IA-5653 (Dec. 22, 2020) (Adopting Release); Sections 203(e) and 203(k) of the Advisers Act (remedial sanctions and cease-and-desist authority)

fact_pattern:
Marcus Tierney, age 41, a resident of Naperville, Illinois, operates a small investment advisory practice called Condor Capital Strategies LLC, registered as an investment adviser with the State of Illinois since 2019. From January 2022 through the present, Tierney has managed a pooled investment vehicle — the Condor Enhanced Income Fund — which deploys options strategies, primarily iron condors on the S&P 500 index, on behalf of approximately 45 accredited investors who have collectively contributed $2.8 million.

Tierney's marketing materials and pitch deck describe the iron condor strategy as 'a market-neutral, defined-risk approach designed to generate consistent monthly income with a historically high probability of profit.' The materials include a backtest showing that the strategy would have produced positive returns in 89% of months over the prior ten years, with an annualized return of approximately 18%. However, the backtest was conducted using mid-price fills (not actual execution prices), did not account for transaction costs or slippage, and assumed position sizing that Tierney does not always replicate in live trading. A footnote in small print states: 'Hypothetical results have inherent limitations and do not represent actual trading. Past performance is not indicative of future results.'

During investor calls, Tierney frequently tells prospective investors that the strategy has 'built-in protection' because iron condors involve selling options that are 'far out of the money' and that 'the math is heavily in our favor.' He does not explicitly promise to double investors' money, but he has told several investors that he 'expects to generate 15-20% annually with limited downside' and that he maintains a 'reserve allocation' to manage adverse moves. In reality, the reserve allocation is approximately 8% of fund assets held in Treasury bills — a figure that a risk management expert might consider inadequate given the tail risk inherent in short options strategies.

In late 2023, a sharp market dislocation caused the fund to lose 31% in a single month. Tierney sent investors an update letter acknowledging the loss but attributing it to 'unprecedented and statistically anomalous market conditions' and reassuring them that 'our risk framework remains intact.' He did not disclose that he had deviated from his stated strategy during the volatility event by rolling losing positions into wider strikes and longer expirations — effectively doubling down on the losing trades rather than closing them at the defined-risk stop-loss levels described in the fund's offering memorandum. The fund has since partially recovered but remains down 14% from its high-water mark. Tierney continues to collect his 2% management fee and 20% performance fee (the latter only on new profits above the high-water mark). No investor funds have been misappropriated, and all account statements accurately reflect actual trading results and balances.
analysis:
The SEC's case against Pallek involved clear-cut fraud: fabricated account statements, Ponzi payments, and outright lies about fund performance. Tierney's situation is materially different — his account statements are accurate, no investor funds are misappropriated, and he operates a legitimate trading strategy. However, several aspects of his conduct raise serious questions under Sections 206(1), 206(2), and 206(4) of the Advisers Act and Rule 206(4)-8. The backtest presentation, while technically disclaimed, may constitute a misleading communication under the SEC's Marketing Rule (Rule 206(4)-1 as amended in 2022) if the hypothetical performance is not presented in a manner that is fair and balanced, or if the assumptions underlying the backtest are not prominently disclosed. Tierney's verbal representations about 'limited downside' and 'built-in protection,' when combined with an arguably inadequate reserve allocation and the actual tail-risk exposure of short options, could be viewed as materially misleading omissions — a classic Section 206(2) theory that does not require scienter.

On the defense side, Tierney's counsel would argue that iron condors are, by definition, defined-risk trades; that the backtest disclaimer satisfies legal requirements; that verbal characterizations of the strategy as 'high probability' are factually accurate (short out-of-the-money options do expire worthless most of the time); and that the 2023 loss, while painful, is the type of tail event that any sophisticated investor in options strategies should anticipate. The deviation from the offering memorandum's stop-loss provisions is the most problematic fact, but defense counsel would characterize it as a real-time risk management judgment call — not fraud — especially since the positions ultimately partially recovered. The absence of any misappropriation or fabricated statements distinguishes this case categorically from Pallek-type enforcement actions.
why_borderline: This scenario sits in the gray zone because it involves a legitimate investment strategy with accurate reporting, but combines potentially misleading marketing (optimistic backtests, verbal minimization of risk), arguably inadequate risk reserves, and an undisclosed deviation from stated risk management protocols during a stress event. None of these facts alone would clearly constitute fraud, but in combination they create a pattern that regulators might view as a breach of fiduciary duty under the anti-fraud provisions of the Advisers Act. The key ambiguity is whether Tierney's conduct reflects the kind of fraud or deception targeted by Sections 206(1)-(2) and Rule 206(4)-8, or whether it represents aggressive-but-lawful marketing combined with a defensible (if imperfect) exercise of investment discretion. Reasonable compliance professionals and enforcement attorneys would disagree on whether this crosses the line.
borderline_factors: Backtest uses favorable assumptions (mid-price fills, no transaction costs) but includes a standard hypothetical performance disclaimer — raising the question of whether the disclaimer is sufficient to cure what may be a materially misleading presentation under the amended Marketing Rule

Verbal representations about 'limited downside' and 'built-in protection' are arguably factually grounded in the mechanics of iron condors but may omit material information about tail risk and the inadequacy of the reserve allocation relative to maximum potential loss

The undisclosed deviation from the offering memorandum's stated stop-loss procedures during the market dislocation could be characterized either as a material omission (failure to disclose a change in strategy) or as a reasonable exercise of portfolio management discretion in rapidly evolving market conditions

No misappropriation, no fabricated statements, and no Ponzi payments — distinguishing this from clear-cut fraud cases like Pallek — but the cumulative effect of optimistic marketing, inadequate reserves, and strategy drift may constitute a pattern of negligent or reckless misrepresentation sufficient for Section 206(2) liability
likely_outcome: A regulator would most likely pursue this as a settled administrative action rather than a litigated fraud case. The SEC or state regulator would probably frame the case primarily under Section 206(2) of the Advisers Act (which requires only negligence) and the Marketing Rule, focusing on the misleading backtest presentation and the failure to disclose the deviation from stated risk management protocols. Tierney would likely settle for a censure, a civil penalty in the range of $75,000-$200,000, an undertaking to retain an independent compliance consultant, and possibly a suspension of 12-18 months rather than a permanent bar. The absence of misappropriation and the accuracy of account statements make a permanent bar or industry-wide ban — like the one imposed on Pallek — disproportionate. A skilled defense lawyer could likely negotiate this outcome down further if Tierney self-reported and remediated the marketing materials. However, if the SEC chose to litigate, the deviation from the offering memorandum's stop-loss provisions without disclosure would be the most damaging fact, as it undercuts the 'defined-risk' narrative central to Tierney's marketing.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act §§206(1), 206(2), 206(4); Rule 206(4)-1 (Marketing Rule, as amended 2022, including requirements for hypothetical performance presentations); Rule 206(4)-8 (prohibiting misleading statements to investors in pooled investment vehicles); Securities Act §17(a); Exchange Act §10(b) and Rule 10b-5 (if the SEC characterizes the fund interests as securities); SEC guidance on performance advertising and backtesting (IA Release No. 6165, 2022); fiduciary duty to disclose material deviations from stated investment strategy

fact_pattern:
Meridian Capital Advisors, LLC ('Meridian') is a registered investment adviser based in Chicago, Illinois, managing approximately $1.2 billion across three private funds: Meridian Strategic Alpha Fund LP, Meridian Credit Opportunities Fund LP, and Meridian Volatility Arbitrage Fund LP. Meridian's chief compliance officer, Sarah Chen, has maintained a rigorous compliance calendar, and the firm has historically filed timely Form ADV amendments.

In December 2023, Meridian's independent auditor, Whitfield & Associates LLP, informed Meridian's CFO, David Park, that the audit of the Meridian Strategic Alpha Fund for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2023, would be delayed beyond the 120-day deadline prescribed by the Custody Rule. Whitfield cited difficulties in obtaining third-party valuations for several complex, bespoke derivative positions held by the fund. Park immediately engaged a secondary valuation firm, Garrison Analytics, to provide independent pricing support to accelerate the process. Whitfield indicated it expected to complete the audit within 30-45 additional days beyond the deadline.

Chen flagged the issue internally and debated whether Meridian was required to promptly amend its Form ADV to disclose that the fund's audit would not be completed on time. Chen consulted outside counsel at Bradford Shaw LLP, who advised that the obligation to 'promptly' amend was triggered, but that 'promptly' allowed a reasonable period for investigation and confirmation — and that since Whitfield had not formally declared an inability to complete the audit but rather projected a delay, the triggering event had not yet crystallized. Chen documented the legal advice and decided to wait until the 120-day deadline actually passed before filing the amendment, reasoning that Whitfield might still accelerate and meet the deadline.

Whitfield did not meet the deadline. The audit was completed 38 days late. Meridian filed its Form ADV amendment 5 business days after the 120-day deadline passed, disclosing the delay. No investors redeemed during the interim period, and no investor complaints were received. The SEC's Division of Examinations discovered during a routine examination that Meridian had known of the likely delay approximately 60 days before the deadline but had not amended its Form ADV until after the deadline lapsed. The SEC staff referred the matter to the Division of Enforcement, questioning whether Meridian violated Section 204(a) and Rule 204-1(a) by failing to 'promptly' amend its Form ADV when it first learned of the expected audit delay.
analysis:
The SEC's position would rely heavily on the QVR precedent and the plain language of Rule 204-1(a), which requires advisers to amend Form ADV 'promptly' when information becomes materially inaccurate. The staff would argue that 'promptly' means as soon as the adviser has reason to believe the previously disclosed information — that the fund would receive a timely audit — is no longer accurate. Under this reading, Meridian's obligation was triggered in December 2023 when Whitfield communicated the expected delay, not when the 120-day deadline actually passed. The SEC could point to the QVR enforcement action as establishing that the Commission takes a dim view of advisers who delay amendments related to audit timing, even when the underlying conduct is largely administrative rather than fraudulent. The staff might also argue that the reliance on outside counsel does not excuse the violation, since the legal advice itself was premised on an arguably strained reading of 'promptly.'

Meridian's defense would center on several strong arguments. First, the triggering event — the actual failure to complete a timely audit — had not yet occurred when Chen was deliberating; at that point, the auditor had communicated a risk of delay, not a certainty. Amending Form ADV to disclose that a fund 'may not' receive a timely audit when the auditor is still actively working to meet the deadline could itself be misleading, potentially alarming investors unnecessarily about an event that might not materialize. Second, Meridian acted in good faith, documented its decision-making, sought outside counsel, and filed the amendment within 5 business days of the triggering event actually occurring. Third, 'promptly' is an inherently flexible standard, and reasonable compliance professionals could disagree about whether the December communication constituted a sufficiently definitive event to trigger the amendment obligation. Meridian would argue that the SEC is effectively imposing a strict-liability, precautionary-filing requirement that the rule's text does not support.
why_borderline: The core ambiguity lies in the meaning of 'promptly' under Rule 204-1(a) when the triggering event is prospective and uncertain rather than a fait accompli. The auditor communicated a likely delay, not an absolute inability to complete the audit on time. Meridian took affirmative remedial steps (engaging a secondary valuation firm) that could have resolved the delay. The question of whether an anticipated future event triggers an immediate filing obligation — versus whether the obligation crystallizes only when the event actually occurs — is genuinely unsettled. Additionally, Meridian's good-faith reliance on outside counsel and its prompt filing once the delay materialized create a credible defense, while the SEC's reading finds support in the prophylactic purpose of Form ADV disclosure and the QVR precedent suggesting the Commission interprets 'promptly' aggressively in the audit-delay context.
borderline_factors: The auditor communicated a probable but not certain delay, creating ambiguity about when the triggering event occurred
Meridian took active remedial steps to accelerate the audit, making the delay genuinely uncertain until the deadline passed
The firm obtained and documented outside legal counsel's advice supporting its interpretation of 'promptly'
The SEC's QVR precedent suggests aggressive interpretation of prompt-amendment obligations for audit-related disclosures, but involved more extended and less justified delays
No investor harm resulted from the 60-day gap between learning of the potential delay and filing the amendment
likely_outcome: The SEC would likely pursue a settled administrative action imposing a censure and a modest civil penalty ($50,000-$150,000 range), similar in structure to the QVR order. The Commission would likely find that 'promptly' required Meridian to amend once it had substantial reason to believe the audit would be delayed — which occurred in December 2023, not at the 120-day mark. However, the mitigating factors — good-faith counsel reliance, remedial steps, prompt post-deadline filing, and absence of investor harm — would significantly reduce the sanction. A contested proceeding would be closer, and an ALJ might credit Meridian's interpretation as reasonable, particularly given the absence of SEC guidance specifically defining the precise moment an anticipated audit delay triggers the amendment obligation. The case would likely settle because litigation risk runs both ways: Meridian risks an adverse precedent expanding 'promptly,' and the SEC risks a ruling that narrows it.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act of 1940 Section 204(a); Rule 204-1(a) (requirement to promptly amend Form ADV); Form ADV Part 1A, Item 7.B and Schedule D, Section 7.B.23 (private fund audit disclosures); Advisers Act Rule 206(4)-2 (Custody Rule, 120-day audit delivery requirement); SEC Release No. IA-6116 (In the Matter of QVR, LLC)

fact_pattern:
Meridian Peak Capital Advisors, LLC ('Meridian Peak') is a registered investment adviser that manages two private credit funds: Meridian Peak Opportunities Fund I, LP and Meridian Peak Strategic Lending Fund II, LP (collectively, the 'Funds'), with approximately $340 million in combined AUM. The firm's founder, CEO, and majority owner is Tobias R. Engstrom, who also serves as the designated Chief Compliance Officer. From 2020 through 2024, Meridian Peak engaged an outside technology consulting firm, DataBridge Solutions, to build a proprietary loan origination and portfolio monitoring platform. The total cost of the platform build was $1.8 million over four years. Meridian Peak allocated approximately 65% of these costs — roughly $1.17 million — to the Funds as 'fund-level technology and portfolio monitoring expenses,' retaining only 35% as a management company expense.

The Funds' Limited Partnership Agreements ('LPAs') contain a provision permitting the Funds to bear 'reasonable organizational, operational, and administrative expenses, including expenses related to portfolio monitoring, valuation, compliance, and technology infrastructure directly supporting fund operations.' There is no specific cap, formula, or detailed methodology prescribed in the LPAs for how shared expenses should be allocated between the adviser and the Funds. The LPAs also state that the General Partner 'shall use its reasonable judgment in allocating shared expenses.'

Meridian Peak's Form ADV Part 2A disclosed, in general terms, that 'certain operational and technology expenses may be allocated to the Funds where they relate to fund operations,' but did not specifically describe the DataBridge platform, the magnitude of the anticipated charges, or the methodology used to determine the 65/35 split. Engstrom internally documented the rationale for the allocation: a time-use study conducted by DataBridge indicated that approximately 60-70% of the platform's functionality was dedicated to fund-level activities (loan monitoring dashboards, covenant tracking, investor reporting modules), while the remaining features served firm-level functions (CRM, marketing analytics, general firm accounting). The Funds' advisory committees — composed of three limited partners from each fund — were briefed orally on the technology initiative at annual meetings in 2021 and 2022, but were not shown the specific cost allocation or asked to formally approve it. Meeting minutes reflect that 'the GP discussed ongoing technology investments to improve portfolio monitoring capabilities.' No LP objected.

In late 2024, a departing limited partner in Opportunities Fund I raised concerns with the SEC's examination staff that the technology charges seemed unusually high relative to the fund's size, and questioned whether Meridian Peak was effectively subsidizing its own business-building through fund assets. The SEC's Division of Enforcement opened a preliminary inquiry.
analysis:
The SEC would likely examine this fact pattern under Sections 206(2) and 206(4) of the Investment Advisers Act, as well as Rule 206(4)-8 (anti-fraud provisions applicable to advisers to pooled investment vehicles). The strongest enforcement argument is that Meridian Peak had a clear conflict of interest — building a proprietary platform that would benefit the adviser's business broadly while charging the majority of costs to the Funds — and failed to adequately disclose the specific nature, magnitude, and methodology of the allocation. The SEC has repeatedly emphasized in enforcement actions (including the Jordaan/One Thousand & One Voices matter and numerous cases under the Private Fund Adviser initiative) that vague, boilerplate disclosure about 'operational expenses' is insufficient when an adviser is making subjective allocation decisions that benefit itself. The fact that Engstrom serves as both CEO and CCO heightens the conflict, as there was no independent compliance function to scrutinize the allocation. The SEC could argue the oral briefings at advisory committee meetings were inadequate because they did not disclose the dollar amounts, allocation methodology, or the dual-use nature of the platform.

The defense would argue that the LPA expressly authorizes the Funds to bear technology and portfolio monitoring expenses, that the 65/35 split was supported by a contemporaneously documented, reasonable methodology (the time-use study), and that the allocation actually under-charged the Funds relative to the study's findings (which showed up to 70% fund-related use). Defense counsel would emphasize that the advisory committees were informed of the initiative and raised no objections, that no LP was misled about the existence of technology charges, and that the Form ADV disclosure — while general — was consistent with standard industry practice for private fund advisers. They would further argue that the SEC is effectively seeking to impose a prescriptive expense allocation standard that does not exist in the statute or rules, and that 'reasonable judgment' as defined in the LPA was exercised in good faith. The defense could also cite the fact that comparable private credit fund managers routinely allocate similar technology expenses to funds, making this an industry-norm practice rather than an outlier.
why_borderline: This scenario sits in a genuine gray zone because: (1) the LPA explicitly authorizes the type of expense at issue but provides no specific methodology, leaving 'reasonable judgment' as the standard; (2) there is a documented, facially reasonable basis for the allocation that a defense expert could support; (3) the Form ADV disclosure, while arguably thin, is not inconsistent with common industry practice for private fund advisers; (4) the advisory committees were informed at a general level but not asked to approve specific amounts; and (5) the SEC's evolving enforcement posture on private fund expense allocation (particularly post-2023 rule proposals and the Jordaan precedent) has created uncertainty about exactly how much specificity is required in disclosures. The core tension is between the SEC's increasingly aggressive stance that advisers must make granular, specific disclosures about every material conflict involving expenses, and the industry's longstanding reliance on broad LPA authorization provisions and general ADV language. A compliance officer would flag the lack of specific dollar-amount disclosure and the absence of formal advisory committee approval, but a skilled defense lawyer would argue that the allocation was authorized, documented, reasonable, and disclosed at a level consistent with prevailing industry norms.
borderline_factors: LPA contains broad but explicit authorization for the category of expense at issue, with a 'reasonable judgment' standard that was facially satisfied
Form ADV disclosure acknowledged technology expense allocation in general terms but omitted specific methodology, dollar amounts, and the dual-benefit nature of the platform
Contemporaneous documentation (time-use study) supports the allocation ratio, but was prepared by the same vendor that received the fees, creating a subsidiary conflict

Advisory committee members were orally briefed but never shown specific figures or asked to formally consent, raising questions about whether 'informed consent' was obtained under fiduciary duty standards
likely_outcome: The SEC would most likely pursue a settled administrative action finding violations of Sections 206(2) and 206(4) and Rule 206(4)-8, focused primarily on the inadequacy of the disclosure rather than the allocation itself. The Commission would likely characterize the Form ADV language as materially misleading by omission, arguing that the adviser failed to disclose the specific conflict of interest (building its own proprietary platform using mostly fund assets) and the magnitude of the charges. However, the penalty would likely be moderate — comparable to or slightly above the Jordaan matter ($250,000 range) — reflecting that the allocation had some documented basis and the LPA authorization was not facially unreasonable. The SEC would probably not characterize this as outright fraud or scienter-based conduct, instead treating it as a negligence-based breach of fiduciary duty under Section 206(2). If litigated, a respondent would have a viable defense, particularly on the question of whether the LPA's broad authorization and the oral advisory committee briefings satisfied the adviser's fiduciary obligations. The outcome would likely hinge on whether the ALJ or Commission views the evolving industry standard for private fund expense disclosure as requiring the level of granularity the SEC now demands, or whether the respondent's practices were reasonable at the time they occurred.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act §206(2) (fraud/deceit by investment advisers — negligence standard); §206(4) and Rule 206(4)-8 (anti-fraud provisions for advisers to pooled investment vehicles); Rule 206(4)-7 (compliance policies and procedures); SEC guidance on private fund adviser obligations regarding expense allocation and conflict disclosure; Commission interpretive releases on fiduciary duty of investment advisers (IA-5248, Feb. 2019); 17 C.F.R. §201.1101(a) (Fair Fund distribution procedures)

fact_pattern:
Meridian Capital Securities, LLC (CRD No. 14522) is a mid-sized broker-dealer headquartered in Parsippany, New Jersey, with 48 registered representatives across five branch offices. The firm primarily conducts a fixed-income business, with approximately 70% of revenue derived from municipal securities transactions with retail customers.

When Reg BI took effect on June 30, 2020, Meridian's Chief Compliance Officer, Sandra Whitfield, adopted a phased implementation plan. By the compliance date, the firm had in place written policies addressing the Disclosure Obligation and Form CRS delivery. For the Care Obligation and Conflict of Interest Obligation, Whitfield drafted a 14-page policy document that outlined general principles — requiring representatives to consider reasonably available alternatives, document cost comparisons for similar securities, and disclose material conflicts — but the document did not include specific procedures for how representatives should document their best-interest analysis, what supervisory review steps principals should follow, or how the firm would monitor compliance with these obligations. Whitfield characterized the document internally as a 'Phase 1 framework' and planned to develop detailed procedures, checklists, and supervisory review protocols by Q1 2021.

By March 2021, Whitfield had developed more granular procedures including a best-interest recommendation worksheet, a conflicts inventory matrix, and a supervisory review checklist for principals. These were rolled out with firm-wide training in April 2021. During the intervening nine-month gap (July 2020–March 2021), the firm's registered representatives continued making recommendations to retail customers in municipal securities.
