In March 2025, the Department of Commerce issues a DPA Title I priority rating (DO-rated order) to Meridian Cloud Systems, Inc., a Virginia-based cloud infrastructure provider, directing the company to prioritize fulfillment of a contract to supply secure computing capacity for a classified Department of Defense supply-chain tracking platform. Meridian's CEO, Sandra Kowalski, complies immediately, reallocating server capacity and delaying deliveries to several civilian customers. Among those delayed is Hargrove Capital Partners, a mid-sized registered investment adviser based in New York that relies on Meridian's cloud infrastructure to run its proprietary algorithmic trading systems, portfolio rebalancing tools, and client-facing compliance reporting dashboards.

Hargrove's Chief Compliance Officer, James Pham, grows alarmed when the infrastructure delays cause a 72-hour degradation of the firm's best-execution monitoring systems and temporarily disable automated Reg BI and fiduciary suitability checks on roughly 14,000 retail client accounts. During that window, several model portfolio rebalancing trades execute without the normal automated compliance overlays, including suitability screens and concentration-limit checks. The trades are consistent with the firm's existing model portfolios and no client suffers realized losses, but three accounts end up with equity concentrations slightly above internal policy limits (62% vs. a 60% cap), and seven trades in retirement accounts proceed without the automated fiduciary-duty flag that would have prompted a human review.

Hargrove's outside counsel, Rebecca Soren of the firm Whitfield & Crane LLP, advises Pham that the DPA compliance was involuntary and that the firm should document the event but that it constitutes a force-majeure-like disruption excusing certain compliance lapses. Pham disagrees and files a voluntary self-report with the SEC, disclosing the 72-hour gap, the specific trades, and the firm's remediation plan. The SEC's Division of Examinations opens a preliminary inquiry, and FINRA separately flags the trades through its cross-market surveillance. Hargrove argues that the DPA-mandated disruption is an intervening cause that negates any finding of willful or even negligent breach of its fiduciary and Reg BI obligations. The SEC staff is skeptical, noting that Hargrove had no documented business continuity plan addressing DPA-related infrastructure reallocation, even though such risks had been publicly discussed in congressional hearings since early 2025.
analysis:
The core legal tension involves whether a federal government action under DPA Title I — which legally compels a third-party vendor to redirect capacity — can excuse or mitigate a registered investment adviser's failure to maintain continuous compliance with its fiduciary obligations under Advisers Act §206, Reg BI under Exchange Act §15(l), and its own internal compliance program under Advisers Act Rule 206(4)-7. Hargrove's strongest argument is that DPA priority ratings are federal mandates with the force of law, backed by criminal penalties for non-compliance, and that a firm cannot be held responsible for downstream effects of lawful government action over which it had no control. This is analogous to force majeure arguments that have found limited but real traction in enforcement contexts, particularly post-9/11 and during COVID-19 market disruptions. The firm also points to the fact that no client was harmed and the deviations were minor and promptly remediated.

The SEC's strongest counterargument is that the duty to maintain adequate compliance infrastructure, including business continuity planning, is non-delegable and anticipatory. The Commission's 2003 compliance rule (Rule 206(4)-7) and subsequent COVID-era guidance explicitly require firms to plan for disruptions to critical third-party service providers. Congressional discussion of DPA reauthorization and its impact on civilian industries was publicly available for months before the incident. The SEC could argue that a reasonably designed compliance program should have identified the risk of DPA-related cloud reallocation and maintained failover capacity or manual override procedures. The lack of a documented contingency plan transforms what might have been an excusable disruption into a compliance program deficiency — a standalone violation regardless of whether the underlying trades caused harm.
why_borderline: This scenario is genuinely ambiguous because it sits at the intersection of two legal frameworks that rarely interact: the DPA's mandatory priority system (which operates with near-absolute federal preemptive force) and the SEC's principles-based fiduciary and compliance obligations (which impose anticipatory duties but have historically been applied with some flexibility during extraordinary disruptions). No SEC enforcement action or no-action letter has directly addressed a compliance gap caused by a DPA-mandated reallocation of a firm's technology infrastructure. The 72-hour window is short enough to seem de minimis but long enough to have affected thousands of accounts. The absence of client harm cuts strongly in Hargrove's favor, but the SEC's increasing emphasis on compliance-program adequacy as a standalone violation means harm is not required. Reasonable compliance professionals and enforcement attorneys would genuinely disagree about whether the firm's failure to anticipate this specific DPA scenario constitutes negligence or is simply an unforeseeable government intervention.
borderline_factors: Whether DPA Title I mandatory priority ratings constitute a force-majeure event sufficient to excuse downstream compliance failures by affected civilian firms

Whether publicly available congressional discussion of DPA reauthorization and civilian-market impacts creates a duty to incorporate DPA disruption scenarios into business continuity planning under Rule 206(4)-7
Whether a 72-hour compliance monitoring gap affecting 14,000 accounts with no realized client losses rises to the level of a material compliance deficiency or is de minimis

Whether the SEC's standalone compliance-program-adequacy theory under Rule 206(4)-7 can attach liability where the root cause is an involuntary federal government mandate rather than a voluntary business decision
likely_outcome: The SEC would most likely resolve this through a negotiated settlement involving a censure and a modest civil penalty (likely in the $150,000–$400,000 range), focused narrowly on the compliance program deficiency rather than the underlying trades. The Commission would likely credit the voluntary self-report and absence of client harm as significant mitigating factors but would decline to recognize the DPA mandate as a complete defense, instead treating it as a foreseeable business continuity risk that should have been addressed. FINRA would likely close its inquiry with a cautionary letter. The resolution would establish a soft precedent that DPA-related disruptions do not automatically excuse compliance obligations, but the penalty structure would implicitly acknowledge the gray zone by imposing consequences well below what a willful or negligent compliance failure of this scope would normally warrant. A court challenge, if Hargrove contested the action, would be closer to 50-50 — a federal judge might find the SEC's position overreaching given the involuntary nature of the disruption.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act of 1940 §206 (fiduciary duty); Investment Advisers Act Rule 206(4)-7 (compliance programs); Exchange Act §15(l) and Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI); Defense Production Act of 1950, Title I §101 (priority and allocation authority); 15 C.F.R. Part 700 (Defense Priorities and Allocations System); Dodd-Frank Act §913 (fiduciary standard study authority); SEC COVID-era guidance on business continuity obligations (2020); FINRA Rule 4370 (Business Continuity Plans)

fact_pattern: In January 2024, Ridgeline Capital Advisors, a dually registered broker-dealer and investment adviser, is engaged by Heartland Community Bancshares ($4.2B in assets) to provide a fairness opinion in connection with its proposed acquisition by Great Plains Financial Group ($18B in assets). Ridgeline's lead banker, Marcus Tolliver, manages the advisory engagement and delivers a fairness opinion to Heartland's board concluding the $37.50 per share offer is fair from a financial point of view. Separately, Ridgeline's wealth management division manages approximately $180 million in retirement and taxable accounts for roughly 1,200 retail clients, many of whom are longtime Heartland customers referred through a longstanding informal relationship with Heartland's branch network. Over the six weeks preceding the public merger announcement, Ridgeline's investment committee — which includes Tolliver in an ex officio capacity — approves a model portfolio rebalancing that increases the weighting of mid-cap regional bank stocks across all managed accounts, including positions in Great Plains Financial Group common stock and, for accounts that already held it, additional accumulation of Heartland Community Bancshares shares. Tolliver attests that he recused himself from the specific security-selection discussion involving Heartland and Great Plains, though he participated in the broader thematic discussion favoring regional bank equities. Ridgeline's compliance department reviewed the rebalancing through its standard conflicts-screening process but did not flag the Heartland or Great Plains positions because the firm's information barrier policy only restricts trading in securities for which the firm is acting as underwriter, not fairness opinion engagements. After the merger is announced and Heartland shares jump 22%, several retail clients realize gains, and a whistleblower complaint is filed with the SEC alleging that Ridgeline breached its fiduciary duty to retail clients and potentially facilitated insider trading.
analysis: The SEC would likely examine this under multiple overlapping frameworks. Under the Investment Advisers Act §206(1) and (2), Ridgeline owes its retail advisory clients a fiduciary duty encompassing both a duty of care and a duty of loyalty, which includes an obligation to address or eliminate conflicts of interest. The fairness opinion engagement created material non-public information (MNPI) about a pending merger, and the question is whether Ridgeline's information barrier was adequate. The firm's policy of restricting trading only for underwriting mandates — not fairness opinion engagements — arguably left a gap that a reasonably designed compliance program should have caught, particularly given evolving SEC and FINRA guidance on the scope of information barriers. However, Ridgeline can argue that its barrier policy was facially reasonable, that Tolliver's partial recusal was documented, and that the thematic rebalancing toward regional banks was driven by independent macroeconomic analysis (rising net interest margins, anticipated M&A wave in community banking) that was memorialized before the Heartland engagement commenced. On the insider trading question under Exchange Act §10(b) and Rule 10b-5, the SEC must establish that Tolliver actually communicated MNPI to the investment committee or that his mere presence at the thematic discussion constituted a constructive tip. Tolliver's defense would emphasize that the regional bank thesis was already in development, the specific security selections were made by a portfolio manager with no access to the deal team's restricted list, and that Heartland and Great Plains represented only a small fraction of the overall rebalancing. The Dodd-Frank §913 harmonization framework and Exchange Act §15(l) add further complexity: if the accounts were serviced in a brokerage capacity for some transactions and advisory capacity for others, the applicable standard of conduct may differ, and Ridgeline could argue that certain trades were executed under a broker-dealer standard (Reg BI's 'best interest' obligation) rather than a full fiduciary duty, which would affect the conflicts analysis.
why_borderline: This scenario sits at the intersection of several genuinely unsettled regulatory boundaries: (1) the adequacy of information barriers for non-underwriting investment banking engagements, where neither SEC nor FINRA has issued bright-line rules specific to fairness opinions; (2) the distinction between a constructive tip and legitimate parallel decision-making when a conflicted individual participates in part of a deliberative process; (3) the unresolved harmonization gap between the fiduciary standard under the Advisers Act and the best-interest standard under Reg BI for dually registered firms, which congressional hearings — including those examining federal banking agency merger oversight — have repeatedly identified as a policy gap; and (4) whether the firm's compliance framework, while arguably outdated, was nonetheless 'reasonably designed' at the time of the conduct, given that fairness opinion information barriers represent an evolving area of enforcement focus rather than established doctrine.
borderline_factors: Information barrier policy excluded fairness opinions — gap is arguably negligent but not clearly unreasonable given lack of explicit regulatory mandate
Tolliver's partial recusal was documented but his presence at the broader thematic discussion creates a plausible inference of constructive tipping without direct evidence of MNPI transmission
The regional bank rebalancing thesis had an independent, pre-existing analytical basis that could explain the trades without reference to MNPI
Dual registration creates genuine ambiguity about whether the applicable standard is Advisers Act fiduciary duty or Reg BI best-interest obligation for specific client accounts
likely_outcome: The SEC would likely pursue this as a civil enforcement action focused on the inadequacy of the information barrier and the fiduciary conflict of interest, rather than as a straightforward insider trading case, because proving scienter and actual MNPI transmission to the investment committee would be difficult on these facts. The most probable resolution is a settled administrative proceeding in which Ridgeline consents to findings of Advisers Act §206(2) violations (which requires only negligence) for failure to adopt and implement reasonably designed policies to prevent conflicts arising from its dual advisory/investment banking roles. Tolliver individually might face a negligence-based failure-to-supervise charge. The insider trading theory under §10(b) would likely be dropped or not charged due to the evidentiary challenges around the recusal and the independent analytical basis for the trades. Disgorgement would likely be limited to advisory fees earned on the conflicted accounts during the relevant period, with a civil penalty in the range of $1-3 million for the firm.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act §206(1)-(2); Exchange Act §10(b) and Rule 10b-5; Dodd-Frank Act §913 (harmonization of fiduciary standards); Exchange Act §15(l) (Reg BI best-interest obligation); FINRA Rule 5280 (information barriers); SEC guidance on reasonably designed compliance policies under Advisers Act Rule 206(4)-7; congressional oversight of federal banking agency merger review policies and dual-registrant conflicts frameworks

fact_pattern:
Ridgeline Capital Management LLC is the investment adviser to the Ridgeline Diversified Growth Fund, a registered open-end mutual fund with approximately $2.8 billion in net assets. When Rule 18f-4 took effect, Ridgeline's portfolio managers determined the fund qualified as a 'limited derivatives user' under the rule, meaning its derivatives exposure did not exceed 10% of net assets, and therefore was not required to adopt a full derivatives risk management program or appoint a derivatives risk manager.

Over the 18 months following the compliance date, the fund's derivatives exposure—consisting primarily of currency forwards, interest rate swaps, and S&P 500 index futures used for tactical hedging—fluctuated between 7% and 13% of net assets on any given trading day. On approximately 22 trading days spread across five separate months, the fund's gross notional derivatives exposure briefly exceeded the 10% threshold, with the highest reading at 12.6%. Each exceedance lasted between one and four trading days before the portfolio management team rebalanced positions back below the threshold. Ridgeline's Chief Compliance Officer, Sandra Whitfield, monitored these exceedances and documented them in internal compliance memoranda, each time noting that the breaches were 'temporary and attributable to market movements rather than intentional position-building,' and that the fund's derivatives positions were hedging-oriented rather than speculative.

Ridgeline did not adopt a written derivatives risk management program, did not appoint a derivatives risk manager, and did not begin filing the enhanced Form N-PORT derivatives disclosures required of funds that are not limited derivatives users. Whitfield's position was that the rule's 10% threshold should be evaluated on a 'consistent basis' over time and that occasional, brief exceedances driven by passive market fluctuations—rather than new derivatives transactions—did not transform the fund into a non-limited user requiring a full program. She pointed to what she described as the fund's 'average' or 'typical' exposure level of approximately 8.5% as evidence the fund remained within the limited user exception. No formal SEC guidance addresses how frequently or for how long a fund may exceed the threshold before losing limited derivatives user status.

During a routine examination, SEC staff from the Division of Investment Management flagged the pattern of exceedances and questioned whether Ridgeline had effectively been operating outside the limited derivatives user exception without the required risk management infrastructure. The examiners noted that while any single exceedance might be viewed as de minimis, the cumulative pattern—22 trading days across five months—suggested the fund's derivatives usage was not consistently limited. Ridgeline's outside counsel, Morgan & Pratt LLP, prepared a response arguing that the rule contemplates a principles-based approach, that the fund acted in good faith, and that the SEC's own adopting release acknowledged the possibility of temporary, unintentional exceedances without prescribing a specific remediation timeline.
analysis:
The SEC's strongest argument is textual and structural: Rule 18f-4(c)(4) defines a 'limited derivatives user' as a fund whose derivatives exposure does not exceed 10% of its net assets. The rule does not contain an explicit tolerance band, averaging mechanism, or grace period for exceedances. The plain language suggests a bright-line test, and a fund that exceeds the threshold—even temporarily—arguably fails to satisfy the condition. The SEC could further argue that the pattern of 22 exceedance days across five months suggests a systemic issue with the fund's portfolio construction rather than a truly isolated occurrence, and that the failure to implement a derivatives risk management program during these periods left the fund's board and investors without the protections Congress and the Commission intended when restricting leverage under Section 18 of the Investment Company Act.

Ridgeline's strongest counterarguments draw from the adopting release's own language and regulatory intent. The SEC acknowledged in the release that derivatives exposure can fluctuate due to market movements independent of a fund's trading activity, and the rule requires funds to adopt 'policies and procedures reasonably designed' to ensure they remain within the threshold—suggesting the Commission anticipated some degree of passive fluctuation. Ridgeline maintained such policies, documented exceedances, and took corrective action within days. Requiring immediate, same-day compliance with a full derivatives risk management program every time market movements push exposure above 10%—only to dismantle it days later when exposure naturally recedes—would impose significant operational costs disproportionate to any investor protection benefit and would effectively set the real threshold well below 10%. Moreover, the fund's derivatives were hedging instruments, not speculative leveraged bets, aligning with the investor protection rationale underlying Section 18.
why_borderline: The core ambiguity stems from the SEC's failure to define in Rule 18f-4 or its adopting release exactly how the 10% limited derivatives user threshold operates over time—specifically whether it is a daily point-in-time test with zero tolerance, a principles-based standard permitting brief passive exceedances, or something in between. The rule prescribes policies and procedures to manage compliance but does not specify a cure period, averaging methodology, or maximum number of permissible exceedance days. Reasonable compliance professionals disagree on whether 22 exceedance days spread over months represents a pattern incompatible with limited user status or a normal consequence of managing a portfolio near a bright-line threshold in volatile markets. The hedging nature of the derivatives further complicates matters, as Section 18's leverage concerns are less acute for risk-reducing positions.
borderline_factors: Rule 18f-4 does not specify a cure period, tolerance band, or averaging methodology for the 10% limited derivatives user threshold
The 22 exceedance days were spread across five months and driven primarily by passive market movements rather than new position-building

The fund maintained policies and procedures and took corrective action within 1-4 trading days of each exceedance, consistent with the rule's requirement for 'reasonably designed' compliance procedures
The cumulative pattern of exceedances—while individually brief—could indicate the fund's portfolio was structurally positioned too close to the threshold to reliably qualify as a limited user
likely_outcome: An SEC enforcement action is unlikely, but the examination staff would probably issue a deficiency letter requiring Ridgeline to either (1) adopt the full derivatives risk management program and appoint a derivatives risk manager on a prospective basis, effectively treating the fund as a non-limited user, or (2) reduce the fund's typical derivatives exposure sufficiently below 10% to create a meaningful buffer against passive exceedances. The SEC is more likely to use this as a compliance matter than a sanctions matter, particularly given the absence of formal guidance on exceedance tolerances and the fund's documented good-faith remediation efforts. However, if the SEC wished to establish precedent, it could bring a settled administrative proceeding with no monetary penalty, requiring the fund to implement the full program and using the case to signal that repeated exceedances—even if individually brief—are incompatible with limited derivatives user status. The fund's hedging rationale and good-faith documentation would mitigate but not eliminate regulatory risk.
applicable_standard: Rule 18f-4 under the Investment Company Act of 1940 (17 CFR 270.18f-4); Section 18 of the Investment Company Act (15 U.S.C. §80a-18); Rule 18f-4(c)(4) limited derivatives user exception; SEC Release No. IC-34084 (adopting release for Rule 18f-4); Form N-PORT reporting requirements (17 CFR 274.150); Dodd-Frank Act §913 (fiduciary and regulatory oversight framework)

fact_pattern:
Meridian Financial Partners is a dually registered firm—it operates both as a broker-dealer registered under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and as an investment adviser registered under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. Sarah Whitfield, a financial professional at Meridian, holds both a Series 7 license and is listed as an investment adviser representative. She has approximately 340 retail clients, most of whom signed both a brokerage account agreement and an advisory agreement when they onboarded.

In March 2023, Sarah meets with longtime client David Okonkwo, a 58-year-old manufacturing executive nearing retirement, who has approximately $1.2 million in a fee-based advisory account and $400,000 in a commission-based brokerage account. During a single 90-minute meeting, Sarah reviews David's advisory portfolio and recommends rebalancing toward more conservative fixed-income allocations—advice she provides in her capacity as an investment adviser, for which she charges a 1.1% annual wrap fee. In the same meeting, she then discusses David's brokerage account and recommends he purchase $150,000 in structured notes issued by Greystone Capital, a product Meridian underwrites and on which Sarah earns a 2.8% commission. Sarah does not explicitly state during the meeting that she is 'switching hats' between her advisory and brokerage capacities, though the structured note recommendation is documented internally as a brokerage transaction.

Meridian's compliance manual contains a three-sentence disclosure policy stating that 'the capacity in which your financial professional acts may vary depending on the account and product type' and that 'brokerage recommendations are subject to a suitability standard while advisory services are subject to a fiduciary standard.' This language appears on page 47 of the firm's 62-page client relationship summary (Form CRS). David signed a general acknowledgment of receipt of the Form CRS eighteen months prior but has no recollection of this specific disclosure.

The structured notes subsequently lose 34% of their value within eight months due to a credit event at Greystone Capital. David files a complaint alleging that Sarah owed him a fiduciary duty across the entire relationship, that the structured note recommendation was conflicted and self-serving, and that Meridian failed to adequately disclose the capacity in which Sarah was acting when she recommended the product.
analysis:
David's strongest argument is that the practical reality of his relationship with Sarah was indistinguishable from a unified advisory relationship, and that reasonable investors in his position—as the RAND Report cited in the Laby article extensively documents—cannot and do not distinguish between the brokerage and advisory capacities of a dual-registrant professional. He would argue that the 'hat-switching' occurred within a single meeting without meaningful contemporaneous disclosure, that the buried language in the Form CRS was insufficient to alert him that the fiduciary duty he relied upon did not extend to the structured note recommendation, and that Meridian's financial incentive to sell its own underwritten product (at a 2.8% commission) is precisely the type of conflict that a fiduciary standard is designed to police. Under Section 913 of the Dodd-Frank Act, Congress authorized the SEC to establish a uniform fiduciary standard for broker-dealers providing personalized investment advice, and the legislative history reflects deep congressional concern about exactly this type of investor confusion at dual-registrant firms.

Meridian's defense would emphasize that the regulatory framework as currently implemented legally permits dual registration and capacity-based compliance. The firm would argue it satisfied its disclosure obligations through Form CRS, that the brokerage transaction was documented as such, and that the structured note met the suitability standard (and arguably Reg BI's best interest standard) applicable to the brokerage account at the time of the recommendation. Defense counsel would note that the SEC has never formally adopted a uniform fiduciary standard under Section 913's permissive authority, and that Regulation Best Interest—adopted in 2019—was explicitly designed as an enhanced standard of conduct distinct from and less than the full Advisers Act fiduciary duty. They would argue that retroactively imposing a fiduciary duty on a transaction properly classified as brokerage would collapse the carefully maintained regulatory distinction between the two regimes.

The conflict-of-interest dimension adds further complexity: Reg BI requires broker-dealers to identify, disclose, and mitigate conflicts, but does not require their elimination. Meridian could argue the conflict was disclosed. David could counter that disclosure buried on page 47 of a document signed eighteen months earlier, with no contemporaneous oral disclosure during the meeting itself, fails to satisfy even Reg BI's conflict mitigation requirements, let alone any fiduciary duty that arguably attached given the holistic nature of the relationship.
why_borderline: This scenario is genuinely ambiguous because it sits at the precise intersection of unresolved regulatory tensions that Congress, the SEC, and courts have struggled with for decades. The SEC chose not to exercise its Section 913 authority to impose a uniform fiduciary standard, instead adopting Reg BI as a compromise. The result is a regime where dual-registrant professionals can lawfully shift between fiduciary and non-fiduciary capacities—but the adequacy of disclosure required to effectuate that shift remains deeply contested. The single-meeting context, where Sarah transitions from advisory to brokerage capacity without explicit verbal notice, makes it factually unclear whether David could have understood the change in legal duties. Additionally, whether Meridian's Form CRS disclosure and internal documentation are sufficient to satisfy Reg BI's conflict mitigation requirements—particularly for a product the firm underwrites—is a question on which FINRA arbitration panels have reached inconsistent results. A reasonable compliance officer could view the transaction as properly documented and disclosed; an equally reasonable regulator could view it as a textbook example of the investor confusion the RAND Report identified and that Congress sought to address.
borderline_factors: Absence of contemporaneous, explicit oral disclosure of capacity switch during a single client meeting covering both advisory and brokerage accounts
Buried capacity-disclosure language on page 47 of a 62-page Form CRS signed 18 months prior, with no evidence of client comprehension
Firm's financial incentive from underwriting the recommended structured notes and the 2.8% commission, raising questions about whether Reg BI's conflict mitigation obligations were truly satisfied

Unresolved regulatory gap: Congress authorized but the SEC declined to adopt a uniform fiduciary standard under Dodd-Frank §913, leaving dual-registrant hat-switching legally permissible but practically confusing to investors
likely_outcome: In a FINRA arbitration proceeding, the panel would likely find partially in David's favor—not on the theory that Sarah owed a blanket fiduciary duty across both accounts, but on the narrower ground that Meridian failed to adequately satisfy Reg BI's obligation to mitigate the conflict arising from recommending a firm-underwritten product and failed to provide meaningful contemporaneous disclosure of the capacity shift. Arbitrators have shown increasing willingness to scrutinize the practical adequacy of disclosures rather than accepting technical compliance at face value, particularly where the client is a pre-retiree and the product is complex. However, the panel would likely reduce damages to account for David's own sophistication as a manufacturing executive and his general awareness of the brokerage account's existence. If the SEC brought an enforcement action, it would likely focus on Reg BI's Care and Conflict of Interest obligations rather than attempting to impose a full fiduciary standard on the brokerage transaction, as the Commission has been cautious about blurring the BD/IA distinction it intentionally preserved when adopting Reg BI. The outcome would hinge heavily on the specific facts of what was said during the meeting and whether Meridian could demonstrate any additional conflict mitigation steps beyond the boilerplate Form CRS language.
applicable_standard: Dodd-Frank Act §913 (authority for uniform fiduciary standard); Securities Exchange Act §15(l) (standards of care for brokers); SEC Regulation Best Interest (Rule 15l-1), including the Care Obligation, Conflict of Interest Obligation, and Disclosure Obligation; Investment Advisers Act §206 (antifraud/fiduciary duty for advisory capacity); FINRA Rule 2111 (suitability, to extent pre-Reg BI conduct is at issue); SEC Form CRS (Relationship Summary) requirements under Rule 17a-14; SEC Release No. 34-86031 (Reg BI Adopting Release, discussing dual-registrant obligations and capacity disclosure)

fact_pattern:
Marcus Ellison is the founder and principal of Ridgeline Capital Advisors, a firm dually registered as both an investment adviser under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 and a broker-dealer under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. Ridgeline serves approximately 2,400 retail clients, most of whom maintain both advisory accounts (charged asset-based fees) and brokerage accounts (charged commissions). In early 2024, Ridgeline began offering clients access to a curated selection of digital asset investment products, including shares in spot Bitcoin ETFs, Grayscale trusts, and a small number of tokenized securities issued on blockchain platforms by emerging companies.

Ellison personally developed a 'Digital Asset Allocation Framework' that Ridgeline's registered representatives use when recommending digital asset products to clients. The framework segments clients into three tiers based on net worth and stated risk tolerance, and assigns maximum digital asset allocation percentages (5%, 10%, or 15%) for each tier. When clients execute digital asset trades in their brokerage accounts, representatives apply Regulation Best Interest's best interest standard and document a basis for the recommendation. When the same products are purchased in fee-based advisory accounts, representatives apply the fiduciary standard under the Advisers Act. However, Ridgeline's compliance manual does not clearly delineate different procedures or documentation requirements for the two standards when applied to digital asset products specifically.

In July 2024, following significant price appreciation of Bitcoin, several Ridgeline representatives began recommending that Tier 2 clients (moderate risk tolerance, $500K-$2M net worth) increase their digital asset exposure up to 15%—the maximum intended for Tier 3 (high risk tolerance, $2M+ net worth)—citing 'changed market conditions.' These recommendations were made in both brokerage and advisory accounts, sometimes for the same client. The representatives documented that the elevated allocations were suitable under Reg BI for the brokerage accounts but did not separately document a fiduciary analysis for the advisory accounts. Ridgeline's Chief Compliance Officer, Dana Whitfield, flagged the practice in an internal review but ultimately concluded that because the Digital Asset Allocation Framework was 'principles-based' and the representatives had documented their reasoning (even if only under the Reg BI framework), the firm was in substantial compliance. No client complaints have been filed, and the digital asset positions have since appreciated further.

The SEC's Division of Examinations, during a routine examination in September 2024, identifies the pattern and questions whether Ridgeline failed to satisfy its fiduciary duty to advisory clients by conflating the Reg BI and fiduciary standards, particularly in the context of volatile digital asset products where the SEC has repeatedly emphasized regulatory uncertainty. Examiners also question whether the firm's uniform 'Digital Asset Allocation Framework' adequately accounts for the distinct obligations owed in each account type, and whether the mid-year deviation from the framework's own tier-based limits constitutes a breach.
analysis:
The SEC would likely argue that Ridgeline violated its fiduciary duty under Section 206 of the Investment Advisers Act by failing to maintain distinct compliance processes for advisory versus brokerage accounts, particularly for digital asset products that carry heightened regulatory uncertainty. The Commission's position—articulated in its June 2019 interpretation of the fiduciary standard and reinforced in Reg BI's adopting release—is that the adviser's fiduciary duty is fundamentally different from and more stringent than Reg BI's best interest obligation. By using a single documentation framework that tracked only Reg BI requirements, Ridgeline arguably failed to demonstrate that it engaged in the ongoing duty of loyalty and care owed to advisory clients, including the obligation to monitor positions and provide advice in the client's best interest over time rather than merely at the point of recommendation. The SEC could also argue that the Digital Asset Allocation Framework's deviation—allowing moderate-risk clients to receive aggressive-tier allocations without enhanced justification—evidences inadequate policies and procedures under Rule 206(4)-7.

Ridgeline's defense would center on the substantive reasonableness of its conduct. The firm would argue that the underlying analysis—market conditions, client financial profiles, documented rationale—satisfied both standards simultaneously, even if the paperwork did not formally separate the two. Defense counsel would cite the SEC's own acknowledgment in the Reg BI adopting release that substantial overlap exists between the two standards, and that a recommendation satisfying Reg BI's care obligation will in many cases also satisfy the fiduciary standard. The firm would further argue that the Digital Asset Allocation Framework was never intended as a rigid constraint but as guidance, and that representatives exercised professional judgment in adjusting allocations—exactly the kind of individualized analysis the fiduciary standard contemplates. The absence of client harm and the subsequent appreciation of positions would be offered as evidence of good faith. Finally, Ridgeline would invoke the broader regulatory ambiguity around digital assets, arguing that in the absence of clear SEC guidance on how fiduciary obligations apply specifically to digital asset products, the firm's principles-based approach was reasonable.
why_borderline: This scenario sits at the precise intersection of three unresolved regulatory tensions: (1) the still-debated practical differences between Reg BI and the fiduciary standard when applied to the same product recommendations, where the SEC has acknowledged overlap but insisted on conceptual distinctness without providing granular guidance on how documentation must differ; (2) the ongoing absence of a comprehensive SEC regulatory framework for digital assets, which makes it genuinely unclear what 'enhanced' fiduciary procedures for digital asset products should look like; and (3) the question of whether a principles-based compliance framework that produces substantively reasonable outcomes can satisfy fiduciary obligations even if it lacks formal procedural separation between account types. The firm's CCO affirmatively reviewed the practice and reached a good-faith conclusion—a fact that cuts both ways, as it shows the firm was aware of the issue but also that it exercised compliance judgment.
borderline_factors: The SEC has acknowledged substantial overlap between Reg BI and the fiduciary standard but has never issued definitive guidance on what distinct documentation is required when the same product is recommended in both account types for the same client

The Digital Asset Allocation Framework deviation was based on articulated market reasoning and applied uniformly rather than selectively, making it difficult to characterize as a breach of loyalty versus a potentially reasonable exercise of investment judgment

The SEC's own failure to provide clear regulatory guidance on digital asset classification and fiduciary treatment undermines an enforcement theory premised on the firm's inadequate digital-asset-specific procedures

The CCO's affirmative review and good-faith compliance determination creates a genuine question about whether the firm maintained 'reasonably designed' policies under Rule 206(4)-7 even if those policies were imperfect
likely_outcome: The SEC would most likely resolve this through an examination deficiency letter or risk alert rather than a formal enforcement action, absent client harm or evidence of conflicts of interest. The examiners would require Ridgeline to implement distinct documentation protocols for advisory versus brokerage digital asset recommendations and to formalize procedures for deviating from the allocation framework's tier limits. If the matter were escalated to enforcement, it would likely result in a settled administrative proceeding with modest sanctions focused on compliance failures (Section 206(4) and Rule 206(4)-7) rather than fraud charges. A court reviewing the matter would likely find that while Ridgeline's procedures were deficient, the absence of client harm, the good-faith compliance review, and the genuine regulatory ambiguity surrounding both the fiduciary/Reg BI distinction and digital asset treatment would weigh against severe sanctions. The case would likely become a vehicle for the SEC to articulate clearer expectations rather than to impose significant penalties.
applicable_standard: Investment Advisers Act §206(1), (2), and (4); Rule 206(4)-7 (compliance policies and procedures); Exchange Act §15(l) (Regulation Best Interest); Dodd-Frank Act §913 (study and authority regarding fiduciary standard for broker-dealers); SEC Interpretation Regarding Standard of Conduct for Investment Advisers (June 2019, IA-5248); Regulation Best Interest Adopting Release (June 2019, 34-86031); SEC Staff Bulletin on Standards of Conduct for Broker-Dealers and Investment Advisers (Account-Type Considerations)

fact_pattern:
Meridian Financial Partners LLC is a mid-sized FINRA-registered broker-dealer headquartered in Charlotte, North Carolina, with approximately 185 registered representatives operating across 42 branch offices. In 2021, Meridian's parent company, Meridian Holdings Inc., established a separately registered investment adviser, Meridian Advisory Services LLC, sharing the same office space, branding, and back-office infrastructure. Approximately 120 of Meridian's 185 registered representatives obtained dual registration as investment adviser representatives of Meridian Advisory Services. The firm's marketing materials uniformly describe all client-facing professionals as 'Meridian Financial Advisors' regardless of whether the client's account is a brokerage account subject to Reg BI or a fee-based advisory account subject to the Investment Advisers Act fiduciary standard.

One such dually registered representative, Sandra Whitfield, serves approximately 340 client households. For roughly 60% of her clients, she recommends and executes securities transactions through brokerage accounts under Reg BI's best interest standard. For the remaining 40%, she provides ongoing investment advisory services through fee-based wrap accounts under the Advisers Act fiduciary standard. When onboarding new clients, Whitfield conducts a financial profile assessment and, based on the client's stated preferences for either transaction-based or ongoing advice, recommends one account type over the other. However, several clients have alleged that Whitfield steered retirement-age clients with moderate portfolios ($250,000–$750,000) into brokerage accounts rather than advisory accounts because the anticipated trading commissions on recommended variable annuity and mutual fund transactions would generate higher compensation for Whitfield than the advisory wrap fee would have produced.

Internal compliance records show that Meridian's written supervisory procedures require a 'capacity disclosure' at each client interaction, specifying whether the representative is acting in a broker-dealer or advisory capacity. However, a 2023 FINRA examination found that in 47 of 83 sampled client files, the capacity disclosure was either missing, ambiguous, or presented on a single combined form that clients signed without apparent understanding of the distinction. Meridian's Chief Compliance Officer, Robert Tran, maintains that the firm exceeded regulatory requirements by providing CRS Form disclosures and that the combined disclosure form was designed to reduce 'disclosure fatigue' experienced by clients receiving multiple documents. Tran points to the firm's quarterly compliance reviews and argues that account-type recommendations were suitable under Reg BI because each client received a written rationale for why the selected account type was appropriate given their trading frequency and service needs.
analysis:
The core legal tension arises from the intersection of Dodd-Frank Act §913's contemplation of a uniform fiduciary standard for broker-dealers and investment advisers—which Congress studied but never fully enacted—and the existing bifurcated regulatory framework where Reg BI governs broker-dealer recommendations and the Advisers Act governs advisory relationships. Under Reg BI's Care Obligation (Exchange Act §15(l) and Rule 15l-1), a broker-dealer must act in the client's best interest at the time of recommendation without placing its own financial interest ahead of the client's. The SEC has explicitly stated that Reg BI applies to account-type recommendations, meaning Whitfield's recommendation of a brokerage account over an advisory account is itself a recommendation subject to the best interest standard. If Whitfield's compensation differential materially influenced her account-type recommendation, this could constitute a violation of Reg BI's conflict-of-interest obligation and care obligation. The missing or ambiguous capacity disclosures compound the issue by potentially violating the Disclosure Obligation under Reg BI.

However, Meridian and Whitfield have substantial defenses. The SEC's adopting release for Reg BI acknowledged that broker-dealers are not required to recommend the lowest-cost option and that compensation differentials alone do not establish a violation. If Whitfield's written rationales demonstrate that brokerage accounts were reasonable given each client's anticipated trading frequency—for instance, clients who expected to make infrequent trades might genuinely pay less in commissions than in an ongoing advisory fee—then the account-type recommendation may satisfy Reg BI even if it also happened to benefit Whitfield. Furthermore, the legislative history under Dodd-Frank §913 shows that Congress explicitly declined to impose a uniform fiduciary standard, preserving the transaction-based model as a legitimate alternative. Meridian can argue that the combined disclosure form, while imperfect, was a good-faith effort to communicate capacity and that technical deficiencies in documentation do not retroactively transform compliant recommendations into violations. The firm's quarterly compliance reviews suggest a functioning supervisory system, even if the execution was inconsistent.
why_borderline: This scenario sits in the precise regulatory gap that Congress identified but deliberately left unresolved in Dodd-Frank §913: the tension between the broker-dealer transaction-based model and the investment adviser fiduciary model when the same individual operates under both standards simultaneously. Reg BI requires best interest conduct but explicitly permits the commission-based model to continue, and the SEC has resisted defining exactly when a compensation differential becomes impermissible steering versus permissible business channel selection. The capacity disclosure failures create a genuine question about whether clients understood which standard of care applied to them, but the regulatory framework itself creates this confusion by allowing dual registration with different standards. Reasonable compliance experts would disagree on whether the pattern of account-type recommendations reflects prohibited self-interested steering or defensible professional judgment that brokerage accounts better served clients with moderate, less-active portfolios.
borderline_factors: Reg BI explicitly covers account-type recommendations but does not require recommending the lowest-cost option, creating genuine ambiguity about when compensation-influenced account channeling crosses the line
Congress studied but deliberately declined to enact a uniform fiduciary standard under Dodd-Frank §913, preserving the dual-standard framework that enables this exact type of regulatory arbitrage

The capacity disclosure failures may be procedural deficiencies versus substantive violations—the SEC and FINRA have not clearly delineated when imperfect Form CRS delivery constitutes a standalone enforcement action versus an examination finding

The pattern of steering retirement-age clients with moderate portfolios into commission accounts suggests a systematic compensation motive, but each individual recommendation may be independently defensible based on trading frequency and cost analysis
likely_outcome: A FINRA examination or SEC enforcement staff would most likely pursue this as a Reg BI Care Obligation and Conflict of Interest Obligation matter focused on the account-type recommendation pattern rather than individual transactions. However, the outcome would likely be a negotiated settlement involving enhanced supervisory procedures, remediation of capacity disclosure deficiencies, and a moderate fine rather than a finding of fraud or a bar. The statistical pattern of channeling retirement clients into commission accounts creates an inference of self-interested conduct that shifts the burden to Meridian to demonstrate through contemporaneous documentation that each recommendation was independently justified. The weak documentation (47 of 83 files with deficient disclosures) significantly undermines the firm's defense. A court reviewing this would likely find the disclosure failures actionable but struggle with the substantive account-type question absent clear evidence that specific clients were financially harmed—particularly if Meridian can show that some brokerage clients actually paid less than they would have in advisory wrap fees. The most probable resolution is a settled enforcement action with neither an admission nor denial of wrongdoing, requiring Meridian to conduct a retrospective review of account-type recommendations and offer affected clients the option to convert to advisory accounts with fee credits.
applicable_standard: Dodd-Frank Act §913 (Study and Rulemaking Regarding Obligations of Broker-Dealers and Investment Advisers); Exchange Act §15(l) and Rule 15l-1 (Regulation Best Interest—Care Obligation, Disclosure Obligation, Conflict of Interest Obligation); Investment Advisers Act §206(1) and (2) (fiduciary duty for advisory accounts); SEC Form CRS (Relationship Summary) requirements under Rule 17a-14; FINRA Rules 3110 (Supervision) and 2111 (Suitability, as superseded by Reg BI for recommendations after June 30, 2020); SEC Reg BI Adopting Release (June 2019) guidance on account-type recommendations and compensation conflicts

fact_pattern:
Meridian Retirement Services, LLC is a registered investment adviser that also serves as a third-party administrator (TPA) for approximately 340 defined contribution plans across the Midwest. In 2007, shortly after the Pension Protection Act's investment advice provisions took effect, Meridian developed a proprietary digital platform called 'RetireRight' that provides individualized asset allocation recommendations to plan participants. The platform uses participants' age, salary, account balance, and self-reported risk tolerance to generate specific fund recommendations from the menu of investment options available in each participant's 401(k) plan.

Meridian's CEO, David Kowalski, structured the arrangement carefully. RetireRight's recommendations are generated by a third-party algorithmic model licensed from Optimum Analytics, Inc., an unaffiliated fintech firm. Meridian does not receive any direct compensation from the mutual fund families whose funds populate the plan menus — those menus are selected by each plan's independent investment committee. However, Meridian's TPA fees are calculated as a flat percentage of total plan assets under administration, meaning that as participant balances grow (potentially influenced by RetireRight's allocation guidance steering participants toward equity-heavy portfolios in bull markets), Meridian's revenue increases proportionally. Meridian discloses this fee structure in its Form ADV Part 2A and in the investment advice agreement signed by each plan sponsor.

In early 2024, following a routine audit, the Department of Labor's Employee Benefits Security Administration (EBSA) raises concerns about whether Meridian qualifies for the statutory prohibited transaction exemption under PPA Section 601 (ERISA §408(g)) for the provision of investment advice. The DOL examiner notes that while Meridian uses an independent third-party computer model, the model has never been formally certified by an 'eligible investment expert' as required under one of the two permissible advice arrangements — the 'computer model' approach. Meridian counters that it instead qualifies under the alternative 'fee-leveling' approach because its compensation does not vary based on which specific investment options are recommended to any individual participant. The DOL examiner responds that while fund-specific compensation may be level, the asset-based TPA fee creates an indirect variable compensation structure that incentivizes RetireRight to recommend aggressive growth allocations, which systematically increases Meridian's aggregate fee revenue.
analysis:
Meridian has a plausible defense under the fee-leveling prong of PPA §601. The statute requires that the fiduciary adviser's fees 'do not vary depending on the basis of any investment option selected.' Meridian's TPA fee is a uniform percentage applied to total plan assets regardless of which funds a participant selects — the fee does not change based on whether a participant chooses Fund A versus Fund B. Meridian would argue this is precisely the type of level-fee arrangement Congress contemplated: the adviser has no incentive to steer participants toward particular funds because its compensation is indifferent to fund selection. The DOL's own 2006-2007 guidance emphasized that the fee-leveling approach was designed as a simpler alternative to the computer model approach, and Meridian's structure facially satisfies that simplicity.

However, the DOL can make a compelling counterargument rooted in the economic substance of the arrangement. While Meridian's fee does not vary by investment option, it does vary by total asset level — and an algorithm that systematically favors higher-returning (and higher-risk) equity allocations will, over time, inflate plan asset values and thus Meridian's compensation. The DOL could argue that Congress intended fee-leveling to eliminate conflicts of interest in investment advice, and that an asset-based fee structure reintroduces a structural conflict through the back door. The DOL might further argue that ERISA's general fiduciary duty of loyalty under §404(a)(1) independently requires Meridian to ensure that its advice arrangement does not create systematic incentive misalignment, even if the literal terms of the §408(g) exemption are arguably met. Courts have historically applied functional economic analysis to prohibited transaction exemptions rather than permitting formalistic compliance that undermines the exemption's purpose.
why_borderline: The statutory text of ERISA §408(g) defines 'fee-leveling' with reference to fees that do not vary based on 'any investment option selected,' which Meridian literally satisfies. But the asset-based TPA fee creates an indirect, structural incentive that potentially undermines the exemption's anti-conflict purpose without triggering its literal prohibition. There is no definitive DOL advisory opinion, court decision, or regulatory guidance squarely addressing whether an asset-based administrative fee constitutes impermissible variable compensation under the fee-leveling prong when the fee is investment-option-neutral but asset-level-sensitive. The distinction between 'compensation that varies by investment option' and 'compensation that varies by investment outcome' represents a genuine interpretive gap in the PPA framework.
borderline_factors: Literal compliance with fee-leveling language versus functional economic conflict of interest
Absence of direct fund-level revenue sharing or differential compensation by investment option
Asset-based TPA fee structure creates systematic indirect incentive favoring aggressive allocations
No DOL advisory opinion or court ruling squarely addressing asset-based administrative fees under §408(g) fee-leveling prong
Tension between PPA's prohibited transaction exemption framework and ERISA's overarching fiduciary duty of loyalty
likely_outcome: A DOL enforcement action would likely result in a negotiated settlement or consent order rather than a definitive judicial ruling, given the genuine ambiguity. If litigated, a federal court would probably find that Meridian's arrangement creates sufficient compliance risk to warrant heightened scrutiny but may not constitute a clear prohibited transaction violation. The court would likely apply a purposive interpretation of §408(g) and examine whether the asset-based fee creates a material conflict that the fee-leveling exemption was designed to prevent. On balance, Meridian would have a reasonable chance of prevailing on the narrow statutory question — the fee genuinely does not vary by investment option — but the court might condition its holding by requiring additional safeguards, such as independent fiduciary oversight of the algorithm's allocation methodology or a cap on equity allocation recommendations. The DOL would likely use this case to propose clarifying regulations rather than rely solely on enforcement.
applicable_standard: ERISA §408(g) (added by PPA §601); ERISA §406(b) prohibited transactions; ERISA §404(a)(1)(A)-(B) fiduciary duties of loyalty and prudence; PPA §601 investment advice exemption (computer model and fee-leveling approaches); DOL Field Assistance Bulletin 2007-01; Dodd-Frank Act §913 (standard of care harmonization study context); 29 C.F.R. §2550.408g-1

fact_pattern:
Meridian Wealth Partners LLC is a dual-registrant—both an SEC-registered investment adviser and a broker-dealer—serving primarily pre-retirees and recent retirees in the Midwest. Marcus Chen, a financial professional dually registered as an investment adviser representative and a registered representative, has approximately 420 clients. In January 2024, Marcus meets with longtime brokerage client Patricia Hollowell, age 62, who has a $640,000 401(k) at her employer, Denton Manufacturing, from which she is about to retire. Denton's 401(k) plan offers a lineup of 22 institutional-class index and target-date funds with an average all-in expense ratio of 0.07%, and the plan's recordkeeper charges a flat $48/year administrative fee. Marcus recommends Patricia roll her 401(k) into an IRA at Meridian, where he would manage the assets on a fee-based advisory platform charging 1.10% annually ($7,040/year). He proposes a diversified portfolio of eight mutual funds, six of which are offered by three asset managers that participate in Meridian's revenue-sharing program, contributing between 10 and 25 basis points to Meridian from their own fees. The revenue-sharing payments are disclosed in Meridian's Form ADV Part 2A under 'Other Financial Industry Activities and Affiliations,' in a paragraph stating that 'certain mutual fund families provide revenue-sharing payments to Meridian or its affiliates, which creates a conflict of interest.' The disclosure does not identify which specific fund families participate or quantify the revenue-sharing amounts.

Marcus documents his rollover recommendation in a one-page internal form. The form notes Patricia's stated desire for 'professional management and comprehensive financial planning,' her moderate risk tolerance, and that the IRA would give her access to a 'broader investment universe' and 'consolidated account management.' The form does not contain a quantitative comparison of fees in the 401(k) versus the proposed IRA, nor does it discuss the specific services Patricia would gain relative to what the 401(k) plan already offered (which included free access to a plan-level financial wellness advisor through Denton's plan). Marcus verbally tells Patricia that 'staying in the 401(k) is always an option' but does not provide a written comparison. Patricia signs a rollover authorization and advisory agreement the same day.

Six months later, an SEC examiner reviewing Meridian's rollover practices flags Marcus's recommendation to Patricia. The examiner notes that (1) the cost differential between the 401(k) and the IRA is substantial, (2) the revenue-sharing arrangement incentivized both the rollover and the specific fund selection, (3) the disclosure of the revenue-sharing conflict was generic rather than specific, and (4) the documentation of the recommendation's basis lacks a meaningful cost-benefit analysis. Meridian's Chief Compliance Officer responds that the firm updated its rollover procedures in 2023 to include the internal form, that Marcus considered Patricia's holistic financial situation, and that the IRA provided materially better service including tax planning, estate coordination, and quarterly portfolio reviews that the 401(k) could not offer.
analysis:
From the SEC staff's perspective—drawing on the 2022 Conflicts Staff Bulletin, the 2019 Guidance on financial conflicts, and the Commission's Interpretation of the adviser fiduciary standard—this scenario raises serious concerns under both the duty of care and the duty of loyalty. The Care Obligation under Reg BI (applicable to Marcus in his broker-dealer capacity for the rollover recommendation) and the parallel fiduciary duty of care (applicable under the Advisers Act for ongoing advisory services) both require a reasonable basis for believing the recommendation is in the customer's best interest. SEC staff bulletins have specifically identified rollovers as a context where the cost comparison between remaining in a plan and rolling over must be rigorously evaluated and documented. The roughly 100x cost increase ($48/year plus minimal fund expenses versus approximately $7,500/year all-in) is the type of 'red flag' that staff guidance suggests demands heightened scrutiny and robust justification. The revenue-sharing arrangement compounds the concern: under the Conflict of Interest obligation, the firm must identify, disclose, and mitigate or eliminate conflicts. The generic ADV disclosure arguably fails to provide the specificity that recent staff guidance contemplates—clients should understand how the conflict actually affects them.

Meridian's defense is not frivolous, however. The Advisers Act fiduciary standard and Reg BI's Care Obligation do not mandate that the lowest-cost option must always prevail. The SEC's own Interpretation acknowledges that an adviser may recommend a more expensive option if additional services, superior investment selection, or holistic planning justify the higher cost. Marcus can argue that Patricia affirmatively desired professional management, that the services available through the IRA—personalized tax-loss harvesting, estate planning coordination, quarterly reviews, broader asset class access—were materially distinct from the 401(k)'s generic financial wellness advisor. The rollover form, while imperfect, documented a rationale. Moreover, Meridian disclosed the revenue-sharing conflict in Form ADV, and courts have not yet established a bright-line requirement for fund-family-specific or basis-point-level disclosure of revenue-sharing in the advisory context. The question becomes whether 'good enough' documentation and disclosure satisfy the standard, or whether the confluence of high cost differential and undisclosed magnitude of revenue-sharing tips the balance toward a violation.
why_borderline: This scenario is genuinely ambiguous because the legal standards at issue—Reg BI's Care and Conflict of Interest obligations, and the Advisers Act fiduciary duties—are principles-based rather than prescriptive. The SEC has never adopted a rule requiring a specific quantitative cost comparison for rollovers, and the staff bulletins are explicitly non-binding. Reasonable experts disagree about how specific revenue-sharing disclosures must be, whether a 100x cost increase can ever be justified by enhanced services, and whether verbal discussion of alternatives satisfies the obligation to consider reasonably available alternatives. The facts support both a finding that Marcus conducted a genuine (if poorly documented) best-interest analysis and a finding that the economic incentives drove the recommendation with only post-hoc rationalization.
borderline_factors: Substantial cost differential (~100x) between 401(k) and proposed IRA that is not quantitatively documented but may be justified by materially different services
Revenue-sharing conflict is disclosed in Form ADV but only generically—not fund-family-specific or quantified—and no staff bulletin or rule specifies the required granularity
Rollover documentation exists but lacks the comparative fee analysis that SEC exam staff increasingly expect, while no formal rule mandates a specific documentation format

Client expressed desire for professional management and signed same-day, raising questions about whether informed consent was truly obtained versus whether the client was steered by a trusted advisor with misaligned incentives
likely_outcome: In the current enforcement environment, the SEC would likely issue a deficiency letter citing inadequate documentation and insufficiently specific conflict disclosure, with a strong possibility of escalation to an enforcement referral if the pattern extends beyond Patricia to a broader book of business. A settled enforcement action would likely result in disgorgement of revenue-sharing payments and a civil penalty, framed around the failure to adequately mitigate the conflict and the insufficient cost-benefit documentation. However, if this were litigated, Meridian would have colorable defenses: the legal standards are principles-based, the disclosure existed, and the client's stated preferences supported the recommendation. A court might find the conduct deficient but not fraudulent, potentially limiting remedies. An arbitration panel in a customer dispute would likely split the difference, finding the recommendation unsuitable or not in best interest based on the cost disparity and awarding partial damages, while acknowledging that some enhanced services were provided.
applicable_standard: Reg BI Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii) (Care Obligation); Reg BI Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(iii) (Conflict of Interest Obligation); Exchange Act §15(l); Investment Advisers Act of 1940 §§206(1) and 206(2) (fiduciary duty—duty of care and duty of loyalty); SEC Commission Interpretation Regarding Standard of Conduct for Investment Advisers (IA Release No. 5248, July 2019); SEC Staff Bulletin: Standards of Conduct—Conflicts of Interest (August 2022); SEC 2019 Guidance on Disclosure of Financial Conflicts Related to Investment Adviser Compensation

fact_pattern:
Meridian Wealth Partners is a dually-registered broker-dealer and investment adviser. The firm employs 180 financial professionals, of whom approximately 120 are dually-hatted (registered representatives who are also supervised persons of the investment adviser) and 60 are broker-dealer-only registered representatives. In January 2023, Meridian's marketing department rolled out a firm-wide digital platform called 'Meridian Advisor Connect,' which serves as the primary client-facing portal. All retail customers — whether in brokerage or advisory accounts — access the same portal, which features the tagline 'Your Meridian Advisor is Here to Help' and allows customers to message their assigned financial professional directly.

When a broker-dealer-only registered representative named Kevin Hartwell receives an inbound message from retail customer Diana Reeves through the Advisor Connect portal, he responds with a recommendation to reallocate a portion of her IRA from a money market position into a proprietary target-date fund offered by an affiliate of Meridian. The target-date fund carries a 75 basis point expense ratio and pays Meridian a revenue-sharing fee. Kevin's email signature, auto-generated by the firm's system, reads 'Kevin Hartwell | Financial Professional | Meridian Wealth Partners.' The portal itself, however, still displays the 'Your Meridian Advisor' branding prominently at the top of every interaction screen.

Meridian's compliance team had previously implemented a pop-up disclosure that appears the first time a customer logs into the portal, stating: 'Meridian Wealth Partners offers both brokerage and advisory services. Your assigned financial professional may be acting in a broker-dealer capacity, an investment adviser capacity, or both, depending on the account and service. Please refer to your account agreements for details.' However, this pop-up only appears once per device, can be dismissed with a single click, and does not reappear during subsequent sessions or at the point when a specific recommendation is made. No additional capacity-specific disclosure accompanies Kevin's recommendation to Diana, and Kevin does not verbally or in writing clarify that he is acting solely in a broker-dealer capacity.

Diana Reeves is a 58-year-old retail customer with a brokerage IRA at Meridian. She is not a financial services professional. She later tells an examiner that she assumed Kevin was her 'advisor' based on the portal's branding and believed he was providing advice in a fiduciary capacity. An SEC examination staff reviews this interaction during a routine exam.
analysis:
The SEC's August 2020 FAQs establish that a dually-registered firm may generally use marketing materials referring to its financial professionals as 'advisors' without presumptively violating the Disclosure Obligation — but critically, the FAQs also state that 'additional disclosures to identify capacity may be necessary for the firm and the financial professional using such materials when making a recommendation,' particularly where a financial professional 'is not also a supervised person of an investment adviser.' The question is whether Meridian's one-time pop-up disclosure, combined with Kevin's neutral email signature ('Financial Professional'), satisfies this obligation when the surrounding environment — the portal name, branding, and tagline — persistently signals an advisory relationship.

Meridian's defense would emphasize several points: the firm is legitimately dually registered and therefore permitted to use 'advisor' branding under the FAQ guidance; the pop-up disclosure expressly alerts customers that their financial professional may be acting in a broker-dealer capacity; Kevin's email signature deliberately avoids the term 'advisor'; and the FAQ guidance says the firm-wide 'advisor' language 'by itself' does not presumptively violate the Disclosure Obligation. A skilled defense lawyer would argue that Meridian made a good-faith effort to layer disclosures and that the FAQ guidance does not prescribe a specific format, frequency, or point-of-recommendation disclosure requirement — it merely says 'additional disclosures' may be necessary, leaving considerable discretion to firms.

The SEC staff's counterargument would focus on the totality of the customer experience: a persistent 'Advisor' branding environment, a single dismissible pop-up that never reappears, no point-of-recommendation capacity disclosure, and the recommendation of a proprietary product with revenue-sharing economics that Diana could not meaningfully evaluate without understanding Kevin's capacity and incentives. The staff could argue that the Disclosure Obligation requires 'full and fair disclosure of all material facts relating to the scope and terms of the relationship,' and that a one-time, easily dismissed pop-up is insufficient when every subsequent touchpoint reinforces the 'advisor' framing. The conflict of interest dimension — the proprietary fund with revenue-sharing — amplifies the materiality of the capacity confusion.
why_borderline: This scenario sits in a genuine gray zone because the SEC's own FAQ guidance explicitly permits dually-registered firms to use 'advisor' branding in general marketing materials while simultaneously requiring 'additional disclosures' at the point of recommendation for broker-dealer-only representatives — but the guidance never specifies the form, frequency, prominence, or timing of those additional disclosures. Meridian did implement a disclosure mechanism (the pop-up), and Kevin's signature avoids the term 'advisor,' which shows some compliance effort. Yet the persistent environmental branding may effectively overwhelm the one-time disclosure, and the absence of any point-of-recommendation capacity clarification — especially when recommending a conflicted proprietary product — could be viewed as a failure to satisfy the 'full and fair' standard. Reasonable compliance professionals and regulators could genuinely disagree about whether the firm's layered approach was sufficient or whether the totality of circumstances rendered the disclosure inadequate.
borderline_factors: The FAQ permits dually-registered firms to use 'advisor' branding generally but requires unspecified 'additional disclosures' for BD-only reps making recommendations — leaving the sufficiency standard undefined

Meridian implemented a pop-up disclosure but it was one-time, easily dismissible, and absent at the point of recommendation — raising questions about whether form and timing matter under the Disclosure Obligation
Kevin's email signature deliberately uses 'Financial Professional' rather than 'Advisor,' showing an affirmative compliance effort that partially mitigates the environmental branding

The recommendation involved a proprietary product with revenue-sharing, creating a conflict of interest that arguably heightens the materiality of capacity confusion and the need for more prominent disclosure
likely_outcome: On examination, SEC staff would likely issue a deficiency letter finding that Meridian's disclosure practices were insufficient to satisfy the Disclosure Obligation under Regulation Best Interest, particularly for broker-dealer-only representatives like Kevin making recommendations through the 'Advisor Connect' portal. Staff would probably stop short of a formal enforcement action on these facts alone, given the firm's partial compliance efforts (pop-up, neutral signature), but would require remedial measures: point-of-recommendation capacity disclosures, redesigned portal language that does not create a persistent advisory framing for BD-only interactions, and enhanced supervisory procedures. If the proprietary fund recommendation were also found to lack a reasonable basis or adequate conflict mitigation, the case could escalate. The likely resolution reflects the SEC's pattern of using exam deficiency findings to establish de facto standards in areas where the rule text and FAQ guidance leave gaps — effectively requiring more than what the firm provided without declaring the firm's reading of the FAQ unreasonable on its face.
applicable_standard: Regulation Best Interest Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(i) (Disclosure Obligation); Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(ii) (Care Obligation); Rule 15l-1(a)(2)(iii) (Conflict of Interest Obligation); Exchange Act Section 15(l); SEC August 2020 Reg BI FAQs on capacity disclosure and use of 'adviser/advisor' terminology by dually-registered firms

fact_pattern:
Meridian Wealth Partners, LLC is a dually-registered investment adviser and broker-dealer headquartered in Denver, Colorado. Its Chief Investment Officer, Sandra Yuen, oversees the firm's model portfolio program, which serves approximately 3,200 retail clients and 14 institutional fund clients, with combined AUM of $2.8 billion. The firm's investment process relies on a quarterly model portfolio review conducted by a four-person investment committee. In Q3 2022, the committee reviewed its moderate growth model—allocated to roughly 1,400 retail clients—and noted that a concentrated municipal bond fund holding (the 'Redstone Muni Income Fund') had experienced a significant ratings downgrade on a substantial portion of its underlying holdings and a 40% increase in its expense ratio following a management restructuring. The committee discussed whether to remove Redstone Muni Income Fund from the model but concluded that the downgrade might be temporary and that the restructured management team had a credible turnaround plan. The committee documented its reasoning in meeting minutes but did not formally update the model allocation or issue any client communication about the retained position.

Over the next two quarters (Q4 2022 and Q1 2023), the committee repeatedly deferred further review of the Redstone position, citing other portfolio priorities and limited analyst bandwidth. During this period, Redstone Muni Income Fund declined 18% in value—underperforming its benchmark by 14 percentage points—and two of its largest municipal bond holdings entered technical default. Meridian's compliance department flagged the position as a 'watch list' item in December 2022 but did not escalate the issue beyond a notation in the firm's internal monitoring system. No client-facing disclosures, Form ADV amendments, or CRS supplements were issued regarding the evolving risk profile of the Redstone holding.

In February 2023, following a routine SEC examination, the Staff raised concerns in a deficiency letter alleging that Meridian may have breached its duty of care by failing to conduct adequate ongoing monitoring of the Redstone position and by failing to act on known material deterioration of the holding. Sandra Yuen responded that the investment committee had affirmatively evaluated the Redstone position in Q3 2022, exercised reasonable professional judgment in retaining it, and that the subsequent performance decline was attributable to unforeseeable market conditions. She further argued that the firm's quarterly review cycle and watch list procedures represented a reasonable monitoring framework, and that the duty of care does not require advisers to guarantee investment outcomes or to rebalance in response to every period of underperformance. Meridian also noted that its Form ADV disclosed that model portfolios were reviewed quarterly and that individual holdings could experience periods of underperformance between reviews.
analysis:
