Meridian's compliance team categorizes all 22 clients as 'professional investors' under Hong Kong's Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO) based on their individual portfolio sizes exceeding HK$8 million, and accordingly applies a lighter-touch suitability assessment consistent with the SFC Code of Conduct's provisions for professional investors.

The portfolios constructed for these clients include significant allocations (35-50%) to illiquid structured products linked to private credit in mainland China, as well as leveraged cryptocurrency fund-of-funds managed by an affiliated entity. The structured products carry a 3-year lock-up and the cryptocurrency allocations are subject to monthly redemption gates. Meridian's Hong Kong suitability process documents each client's investment experience and risk tolerance in a one-page questionnaire but does not assess foreseeable liquidity needs, retirement planning horizons, or the interaction of these products with each client's broader UK-held portfolio. No assessment is conducted under the FCA's Consumer Duty (PRIN 12), which took effect in July 2023, on the basis that Meridian is regulated solely by the SFC and the clients are serviced from Hong Kong.

Six months later, several clients complain that they were not warned about the illiquidity risks in the context of their overall financial position, and that the leveraged crypto allocations were unsuitable given their stated moderate risk appetite. The FCA opens a preliminary inquiry into whether Meridian Group Holdings plc, as the UK parent that referred these UK-resident clients, has obligations under the Consumer Duty and whether Meridian Hong Kong is effectively carrying on regulated activity in the UK through the referral arrangement. Simultaneously, the SFC reviews Meridian's professional investor classification and the adequacy of its suitability processes under paragraphs 5.2 and 5.3 of the SFC Code of Conduct.
analysis:
The central legal tension is whether a Hong Kong SFC-licensed entity servicing UK-resident clients referred by its UK-regulated parent can avoid the application of the FCA Consumer Duty and MiFID II-derived suitability requirements. Under PRIN 12 (Consumer Duty), UK-authorized firms must act to deliver good outcomes for retail customers, and the FCA has signaled that firms cannot circumvent the Duty by routing clients through overseas affiliates where the substance of the relationship originates in the UK. The FCA could argue that Meridian Group Holdings plc's referral activity constitutes an integral part of the distribution chain, making the parent a 'manufacturer' or 'distributor' under the Consumer Duty's product governance framework, and that the parent bears responsibility for ensuring the end-to-end customer journey delivers good outcomes — including by ensuring the overseas affiliate's processes meet equivalent standards. If the referral is deemed to involve a 'communication of a financial promotion' or 'arranging deals in investments' occurring in the UK, the Hong Kong entity itself may be conducting regulated activity in the UK without authorization, engaging Section 21 and Section 19 FSMA issues.

Conversely, Meridian's defense is substantial. The Hong Kong entity is independently licensed by the SFC, the clients signed engagement letters governed by Hong Kong law, and all investment management decisions and client interactions occur from Hong Kong. Under the SFC Code of Conduct, classifying clients with portfolios over HK$8 million as professional investors is explicitly permitted, and the lighter suitability obligations for professional investors are well-established regulatory practice. The IOSCO Suitability Principles (2021) recognize that suitability standards may be calibrated based on client classification, and ASIC's §961B similarly permits reduced obligations for wholesale clients. Meridian can argue the referral was merely an introduction — no advice or financial promotion was communicated in the UK — and that imposing the Consumer Duty extraterritorially would undermine the principle of host-state regulation and Hong Kong's independent regulatory sovereignty. The SFC's own regime is IOSCO-compliant and constitutes a robust, internationally recognized framework.
why_borderline: This scenario sits precisely at the intersection of multiple unresolved regulatory questions: (1) the extraterritorial reach of the FCA Consumer Duty when UK-resident clients are served by overseas affiliates of UK-authorized firms; (2) whether a referral from a UK parent to an overseas subsidiary constitutes 'arranging' or a 'financial promotion' under FSMA; (3) whether Hong Kong professional investor classification is sufficient when the client's circumstances (UK residency, moderate risk appetite, liquidity needs) suggest a more granular suitability analysis is warranted under any reasonable international standard; and (4) whether the SFC's lighter-touch suitability regime for professional investors adequately addresses the IOSCO principle that suitability must account for a client's total financial situation. No regulator has definitively ruled on the Consumer Duty's application to this precise referral structure, and the SFC and FCA have not published joint guidance on how overlapping jurisdiction should be resolved for dual-national clients serviced through intra-group referrals.
borderline_factors: The FCA Consumer Duty's extraterritorial reach to overseas affiliates of UK-authorized firms receiving referred UK-resident clients remains untested in enforcement
Whether the UK parent's referral constitutes 'arranging deals in investments' or a 'financial promotion' under FSMA Sections 19 and 21 depends on factual nuances of the referral communications

Hong Kong professional investor classification is legally valid under the SFO but arguably fails to capture foreseeable liquidity needs and holistic suitability factors emphasized by IOSCO and the FCA Consumer Duty

The 35-50% allocation to illiquid and leveraged products for clients with stated moderate risk tolerance creates a factual suitability tension even under the SFC's lighter professional investor regime
likely_outcome: The FCA would likely assert jurisdiction over Meridian Group Holdings plc for its role in the referral chain and require the UK parent to demonstrate that it took reasonable steps to ensure good client outcomes, potentially resulting in a requirement to enhance due diligence on the Hong Kong affiliate's suitability processes for referred UK clients. However, the FCA would likely stop short of asserting direct regulatory authority over Meridian Hong Kong itself, absent evidence that investment advice or financial promotions were communicated from or into the UK. The SFC, upon review, would likely not find a violation of the professional investor classification but could issue supervisory guidance or a warning letter regarding the adequacy of Meridian's suitability documentation — particularly the failure to assess liquidity needs and total portfolio context — noting that even for professional investors, paragraphs 5.2 and 5.3 of the Code of Conduct require suitability assessments that are reasonable in the circumstances. The most likely resolution is a negotiated outcome where both regulators require enhanced procedures for cross-referred clients without a formal finding of violation, but the UK parent may face a Consumer Duty remediation requirement to compensate affected clients for the information gap.
applicable_standard: FCA PRIN 12 (Consumer Duty, effective July 2023); FSMA 2000 Sections 19 and 21 (regulated activity and financial promotions); SFC Code of Conduct paragraphs 5.2 and 5.3 (know your client and suitability); Securities and Futures Ordinance (SFO) Schedule 1 (professional investor definition); MiFID II Article 25 (suitability and appropriateness); IOSCO Suitability Requirements for the Distribution of Complex Financial Products (2013, revised 2021); ASIC Corporations Act §961B (best interests duty for personal advice)

fact_pattern:
Meridian Wealth Partners LLP is a UK-authorised financial advisory firm that also holds an AFSL (Australian Financial Services Licence) and operates a branch in Frankfurt passported under MiFID II. Meridian's CEO, Claudia Hargreaves, oversees a product governance committee that approved distribution of the 'Aether Multi-Strategy Fund' — a Luxembourg-domiciled UCITS managed by Stellaris Capital Management. The fund charges a 1.85% annual management charge plus a 15% performance fee with a high-water mark, and is distributed to retail clients across the UK, EU, and Australia.

In Q1 2024, Meridian conducted its FCA Consumer Duty fair value assessment for Aether. The assessment concluded that, while the fund's total cost of ownership placed it in the top quartile of expense for its peer group, the fund had delivered consistent first-quartile risk-adjusted returns over a rolling five-year period, and client surveys showed 78% satisfaction rates. Meridian's compliance team documented that the price-to-outcome ratio was justified and that the fund delivered 'good outcomes' within the meaning of PRIN 12. The assessment also noted that Meridian received a 0.45% trail commission from Stellaris, which was disclosed in the fund's KID and in Meridian's own fee schedule, but was not separately itemised in the annual value assessment report sent to clients.

However, a complication arose: ASIC's §961B suitability framework requires that personal advice providers demonstrate that the recommendation is 'appropriate' considering the client's 'relevant personal circumstances,' which Australian courts have interpreted to require granular cost-benefit analysis at the individual client level — not at the product cohort level. Furthermore, MiFID II Article 25 product governance obligations require manufacturers and distributors to identify a target market and ensure ongoing compatibility, with the 2023 ESMA guidelines emphasizing that value-for-money assessments should benchmark against 'comparable products available in the relevant market,' not just the product's own historical performance.

In March 2024, a group of 14 Australian retail clients — mostly retirees with moderate risk profiles — complained to both ASIC and the FCA that the Aether fund was unsuitable given its high fees and volatility relative to simpler index-tracking alternatives. Six UK clients filed similar complaints, arguing that Meridian's value assessment was self-serving because it relied on backward-looking performance data without adequately stress-testing future scenarios or accounting for the compounding drag of fees over the clients' expected investment horizons of 15-20 years. Meridian's defence is that it applied the most rigorous standard — the UK Consumer Duty — uniformly across all jurisdictions, that good outcomes were demonstrably achieved, and that no single regulator's framework was violated.
analysis:
The core tension lies in whether a firm operating across multiple regulatory regimes can satisfy the UK Consumer Duty's outcomes-focused value assessment while simultaneously meeting the more granular, individual-level suitability requirements under ASIC §961B and the comparative market benchmarking expectations under MiFID II/ESMA guidelines. Meridian's position is defensible: the FCA Consumer Duty does not prescribe a single methodology for fair value assessments, and PRIN 12's outcome-based standard arguably gives firms latitude to define 'good outcomes' using historical risk-adjusted performance and client satisfaction data. The trail commission was disclosed, and the fund did outperform on a risk-adjusted basis. The FCA has acknowledged that higher-cost products are not inherently poor value if they deliver commensurate outcomes. Meridian can also argue that applying the Consumer Duty — widely regarded as the most demanding retail conduct standard globally — as a floor across all jurisdictions demonstrates good faith and a culture oriented toward consumer protection.

On the other side, regulators could argue that Meridian's value assessment is materially deficient on multiple fronts. The FCA's own Consumer Duty guidance under PRIN 2A.4 states that firms must consider the 'nature, quality and cost' of a product 'in the round,' and that backward-looking performance alone is insufficient — firms must consider whether the charging structure could foreseeably lead to harm, particularly for clients with long time horizons where fee compounding significantly erodes returns. ASIC would likely find that a cohort-level assessment fails the §961B personal advice standard, which requires demonstration that the specific product is appropriate for each client's individual circumstances, not merely that it performed well on average. ESMA's 2023 value-for-money guidance explicitly requires comparison against comparable market alternatives, and the failure to benchmark against low-cost index alternatives — which may have delivered similar or superior net-of-fee outcomes — is a significant gap. The non-itemisation of the trail commission in the value assessment report, while technically compliant with disclosure rules, could be viewed under the Consumer Duty's 'consumer understanding' outcome as undermining clients' ability to properly evaluate whether the price they pay represents fair value.
why_borderline: This scenario is genuinely ambiguous because Meridian applied a rigorous standard in good faith, the product objectively outperformed peers on a risk-adjusted basis, and disclosures were technically compliant. Yet the firm's value assessment methodology arguably fails to satisfy the forward-looking, individual-level, and comparative-benchmarking requirements that different regulators emphasize to varying degrees. The FCA Consumer Duty is deliberately principles-based and does not mandate specific assessment methodologies, creating genuine uncertainty about whether Meridian's approach is adequate. Reasonable compliance professionals could disagree about whether cohort-level backward-looking analysis satisfies the 'act to deliver good outcomes' standard when applied to retirees with long horizons and moderate risk appetites, and whether the trail commission disclosure regime meets the spirit — as opposed to the letter — of the consumer understanding outcome.
borderline_factors: The fund demonstrably delivered first-quartile risk-adjusted returns historically, but fee drag over 15-20 year retirement horizons was not modeled or disclosed in the value assessment

The FCA Consumer Duty's fair value assessment methodology is principles-based with no prescribed comparative benchmarking requirement, while ESMA's 2023 guidance explicitly requires comparison against comparable market alternatives

ASIC §961B requires individual-level suitability analysis, but Meridian conducted a product-cohort-level assessment and applied it uniformly, raising questions about whether a single methodology can satisfy divergent jurisdictional standards

Trail commission was disclosed in KID and fee schedules but was not separately itemised in the annual value assessment report, creating tension between technical disclosure compliance and the Consumer Duty's consumer understanding outcome requiring information that genuinely enables informed decision-making
likely_outcome: The FCA would likely require Meridian to enhance its value assessment methodology rather than impose sanctions, directing the firm to incorporate forward-looking fee-impact modelling, comparative benchmarking against lower-cost alternatives, and more granular segmentation by client cohort (particularly retirees). The FCA might issue a 'Dear CEO' letter or supervisory finding rather than pursue enforcement, given the genuine ambiguity in methodology requirements and the fact that outcomes were positive in absolute terms. ASIC would likely be more aggressive, finding a breach of §961B for the Australian retiree cohort on the basis that a product-level assessment cannot substitute for individual suitability analysis, and may require remediation or compensation for clients where cheaper alternatives were clearly more appropriate. The MiFID II position would turn on whether the German BaFin or the relevant NCA adopts ESMA's value-for-money benchmarking guidance strictly — if so, a deficiency finding is probable but likely addressed through enhanced product governance rather than sanctions. The critical lesson is that applying the 'highest' standard across jurisdictions does not guarantee compliance with each jurisdiction's specific requirements, particularly where those requirements differ not in stringency but in kind.
applicable_standard: FCA Consumer Duty (PRIN 12, specifically PRIN 2A.4 on fair value and PRIN 2A.5 on consumer understanding); MiFID II Article 25 (suitability and product governance) and ESMA 2023 Value-for-Money Guidelines; ASIC Corporations Act §961B (appropriate personal advice obligation); IOSCO Suitability Principles 2021 (Principles 5 and 6 on suitability analysis and cost disclosure); FCA PROD 3 (product governance for distributors)

fact_pattern:
Meridian Wealth Partners Pty Ltd ('Meridian') is an Australian Financial Services Licensee based in Sydney that provides financial product advice to retail clients. In 2023, Meridian launched 'Meridian Global Insights,' a digital platform offering investment commentary and portfolio model allocations to subscribers across Australia, the UK, and the EU. The platform was developed by Dr. Elena Vasquez, Meridian's head of investment strategy, and uses algorithmic filtering to present content based on each subscriber's self-reported investor profile (age bracket, risk tolerance band, investment horizon, and jurisdiction of residence). Subscribers pay AUD $49/month and complete a brief onboarding questionnaire.

The platform generates weekly 'Insight Reports' that include asset allocation models labeled 'Conservative,' 'Balanced,' and 'Growth,' each naming specific ETFs and managed funds available on major exchanges. Each report carries a prominent disclaimer: 'This is general information only and does not constitute personal financial advice. It does not take into account your individual financial circumstances, objectives, or needs.' However, the algorithmic filtering means a 62-year-old UK-based subscriber who self-identified as 'conservative' with a '5-year horizon' would only see the Conservative model and related commentary, while a 30-year-old Australian subscriber selecting 'growth' and '20+ years' would see only the Growth model. No human adviser reviews individual subscriber profiles or outputs.

In early 2024, Mrs. Patricia Langford, a 67-year-old retired teacher in Manchester, UK, subscribed to the platform and followed the Conservative model's allocation into several Australian-domiciled ETFs. After a 14% drawdown in her portfolio due to currency risk and sector concentration she had not anticipated, she complained to both ASIC and the UK FCA. Mrs. Langford argued the platform effectively gave her personal advice tailored to her circumstances without any of the protections required under ASIC's regime, the UK FCA's Consumer Duty, or MiFID II's suitability requirements. Meridian maintains it provided general advice only, with appropriate disclaimers, and that algorithmic content filtering is no different from a newspaper's lifestyle section sorting articles by reader demographic.
analysis:
The central question is whether Meridian's algorithmically filtered output crosses the line from general advice to personal advice under multiple overlapping regulatory frameworks. Under ASIC's Corporations Act s766B(3), personal advice is financial product advice given where the provider has considered, or ought reasonably to have considered, one or more of the client's objectives, financial situation, or needs. Meridian collected age, risk tolerance, investment horizon, and jurisdiction—data that maps closely to the 'relevant personal circumstances' contemplated by s961B and RG 175's guidance on the general/personal advice distinction. The algorithmic filtering then used those inputs to selectively present specific product recommendations, which arguably demonstrates that the system did 'consider' the client's circumstances in generating its output. Under the UK FCA's Consumer Duty (PRIN 12, effective July 2023), firms must act to deliver good outcomes for retail customers, with particular attention to the Consumer Understanding and Consumer Support outcomes. The FCA's guidance explicitly warns that personalised digital journeys can transform what appears to be general information into a regulated advice service. Similarly, MiFID II Article 25 requires suitability assessments when investment advice is provided, and ESMA has indicated that algorithmic personalisation based on client data may constitute investment advice regardless of disclaimers.

On the other hand, Meridian can argue that its platform merely segments pre-existing generic model portfolios—models that exist independently of any subscriber—into categories that subscribers self-select into. The platform does not assess Mrs. Langford's total wealth, existing holdings, tax position, pension entitlements, or specific financial goals. It performs no holistic analysis. The ASIC guidance in RG 175 recognizes that general advice can be directed at specific audience segments without becoming personal advice, provided the provider does not purport to have considered individual circumstances. Meridian's disclaimers are prominent, and comparable services (e.g., risk-profiled model portfolios published by research houses) have historically been treated as general advice. Furthermore, the cross-border dimension complicates enforcement: Meridian holds an AFS licence but may not be conducting regulated activity in the UK or EU if it has no establishment there, potentially placing Mrs. Langford outside the FCA's and ESMA's direct jurisdiction over Meridian while raising questions about ASIC's extraterritorial reach.
why_borderline: This scenario sits in a genuine gray zone because the technology-enabled personalisation creates a functional experience indistinguishable from tailored advice—the subscriber sees only recommendations filtered to their profile—yet the underlying methodology involves pre-built models segmented by broad demographic bands rather than individualised analysis. Regulators across jurisdictions have signaled increasing skepticism toward disclaimer-based defenses when the substance of the interaction is personalised, but no jurisdiction has drawn a bright line defining exactly when algorithmic filtering of pre-existing models becomes personal advice. The cross-border element further complicates matters: the FCA Consumer Duty's 'good outcomes' standard, MiFID II's suitability framework, IOSCO's 2021 Suitability Principles on digital advice, and ASIC's s961B best interests duty each approach the classification question with slightly different tests and thresholds, making it plausible that the same conduct could be classified differently depending on the jurisdiction applying its own framework.
borderline_factors: Collection of personal data (age, risk tolerance, horizon) that maps to statutory 'relevant personal circumstances' under s961B and MiFID II suitability inputs, despite being used only for content filtering rather than holistic analysis

Algorithmic filtering creates a functionally personalised experience where the subscriber sees only recommendations matched to their profile, blurring the general/personal advice boundary regardless of disclaimers
Prominent disclaimers and the absence of any human adviser review or individualised portfolio construction support the general advice characterisation under traditional RG 175 guidance

Cross-jurisdictional regulatory divergence: ASIC's substance-over-form approach to advice classification may reach a different conclusion than the FCA Consumer Duty's outcomes-focused test or MiFID II's definition of 'personal recommendation,' creating genuine uncertainty about which standard applies and how
likely_outcome: ASIC would likely take the position that Meridian's platform provides personal advice, or at minimum that Meridian 'ought reasonably to have considered' the client's personal circumstances given the data collected and used to filter outputs, triggering the best interests duty under s961B. ASIC has consistently emphasised substance over form and has flagged digital advice models that collect personal data and use it to tailor outputs as crossing the personal advice threshold, regardless of disclaimers. The FCA would likely find a breach of the Consumer Duty's Consumer Understanding outcome, concluding that the platform's design led Mrs. Langford to reasonably believe she was receiving personalised guidance without adequate suitability protections. However, enforcement would be complicated by jurisdictional questions—the FCA would need to establish that Meridian was conducting regulated activity in the UK. A court or tribunal would likely resolve the core classification issue against Meridian, finding that the combination of data collection, algorithmic personalisation, and specific product identification crosses the general advice threshold, but the remedy and enforcement pathway would depend heavily on which regulator pursued the matter and whether cross-border cooperation mechanisms were invoked. The disclaimer defense, while not frivolous, would likely fail under both ASIC's and the FCA's current regulatory posture toward digital advice.
applicable_standard: ASIC Corporations Act s766B(3) (personal advice definition); s961B (best interests duty); RG 175 (financial product advisers—conduct and disclosure, November 2024 edition); UK FCA PRIN 2A/PRIN 12 (Consumer Duty, effective July 2023); FCA COBS 9 (suitability); EU MiFID II Article 25 (suitability and appropriateness); ESMA Guidelines on MiFID II suitability requirements (2023 update); IOSCO Final Report on Suitability Requirements for Distribution of Complex Financial Products (2013, updated principles 2021)
